docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This tutorial was written to accompany the FPGA and ASIC Agents and Skills project — a complete, open-source design pipeline that takes a hardware idea from a text specification all the way to a fabrication-ready GDSII file.

The project exists because chip design has historically been locked behind expensive proprietary tools and non-disclosure agreements. Thanks to efforts from Google, SkyWater Technology, Efabless, and the open-source EDA community, it is now possible for any engineer with a laptop to design and even fabricate a real silicon chip at no cost.

This tutorial assumes you can write code in some programming language and understand binary numbers. No prior hardware or electronics knowledge is assumed. Every concept is introduced with an analogy before any mathematics, and every code listing is taken directly from a real file in the project so you can run it yourself.

Good luck, and happy taping out!

# -- Lint ----------------------------------------------------------------------
verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv

# -- Simulate ------------------------------------------------------------------
iverilog -g2012 -o sim.out uart_16550.sv uart_16550_tb.sv && vvp sim.out
verilator --binary -j 0 --trace uart_16550.sv --exe tb.cpp && ./obj_dir/V*
cd verification/cocotb && make SIM=icarus MODULE=test_uart_16550

# -- Formal verification -------------------------------------------------------
cd eda/symbiyosys && sby -f uart_16550_bmc.sby

# -- Synthesis (Yosys) ---------------------------------------------------------
bash scripts/bash/synth_yosys.sh uart_16550 rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv sky130
yosys -p "synth -top uart_16550; write_verilog netlist.v" uart_16550.sv

# -- FPGA (Vivado non-project) -------------------------------------------------

vivado -mode batch -source fpga/xilinx-artix7/program_arty.tcl

# -- Physical design (OpenROAD) ------------------------------------------------
openroad -exit eda/openroad/uart_16550/floorplan.tcl
openroad -exit eda/openroad/uart_16550/full_flow.tcl

# -- DRC / LVS ----------------------------------------------------------------
klayout -b -r $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/klayout/drc/sky130A.lydrc \
    -rd input=gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.gds \
    -rd report=gdsii/outputs/drc_report.xml
netgen -batch lvs design.ext.spice synthesis.spice \
    $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/netgen/sky130A_setup.tcl lvs_report.txt

# -- Full pipeline -------------------------------------------------------------
make ip IP=uart_16550 TARGET=asic PDK=sky130
make ip IP=uart_16550 TARGET=fpga BOARD=arty_a7_35t

docs.title: Appendix B: Glossary
docs.text: ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit — a chip manufactured for one fixed purpose. AXI4 Advanced eXtensible Interface version 4 — ARM’s bus protocol standard. BMC Bounded Model Checking — formal verification technique that checks properties up to \(k\) clock cycles. CDC Clock Domain Crossing — transferring signals between different clock domains. CLB Configurable Logic Block — the basic cell of an FPGA containing LUTs and flip-flops. CTS Clock Tree Synthesis — inserting buffers to balance clock arrival time across the chip. DRC Design Rule Check — verifying that a layout obeys the foundry’s manufacturing rules. DSP Digital Signal Processing — or the dedicated DSP slice hardware block in FPGAs. FPGA Field-Programmable Gate Array — a chip that can be reconfigured to implement any circuit. FSM Finite State Machine — a circuit that moves between a fixed set of named states. GDS/GDSII Graphic Design System II — the standard file format for chip layouts. HDL Hardware Description Language — a language for describing circuits (e.g. SystemVerilog). IP Intellectual Property — a reusable hardware block (core) with a standard interface. ISA Instruction Set Architecture — the set of instructions a processor can execute. LEF Library Exchange Format — abstract physical description of cells for place-and-route. LUT Look-Up Table — the basic logic element in an FPGA; implements any truth table. LVS Layout vs. Schematic — check that the physical layout matches the logical netlist. MPW Multi-Project Wafer — a wafer run shared by multiple designers to reduce cost. PDK Process Design Kit — everything the tools need to target a specific manufacturing process. PnR Place and Route — placing cells on the chip and routing the connecting wires. RISC-V An open-source instruction set architecture (ISA) with a modular extension system. RTL Register Transfer Level — a hardware abstraction describing data flow between registers. STA Static Timing Analysis — verifying that all signals meet timing requirements. SVA SystemVerilog Assertions — formal properties written in SystemVerilog syntax. WNS Worst Negative Slack — the most critical timing violation; must be \(\geq 0\) to pass. XDC Xilinx Design Constraints — Vivado’s constraint file format (TCL-based).

docs.title: 1.1 What Is This Tutorial About?
docs.text:
Every electronic device around you — your smartphone, laptop, the router providing your Wi-Fi, the satellite navigation system in your car — runs on custom silicon chips. These chips are designed by engineers using a process that starts with a simple idea written in a hardware description language and ends, months later, with a physical piece of silicon being manufactured in a cleanroom the size of a football field.

This tutorial walks you through the entire journey: from the first line of code describing a digital circuit, all the way to a fabrication-ready chip layout, with an FPGA prototype at the halfway point for validation. You do not need prior chip-design experience. If you have programmed a computer before and understand basic binary numbers, you have everything you need to get started.

Analogy: Architect to Builder

Think of chip design like designing a skyscraper.

  • The architect draws blueprints (RTL design).

  • The structural engineer checks that it won’t fall down (verification & formal proof).

  • The construction manager figures out where every beam goes (physical design).

  • The inspector certifies the building is safe (DRC/LVS signoff).

  • The factory pours the concrete and erects the steel (fabrication).

Each stage has its own tools, its own language, and its own specialists. This tutorial covers all of them.

docs.title: 1.2 The Two Worlds: FPGA and ASIC
docs.text: Chip designers live in two worlds, and understanding the difference is the single most important concept in this tutorial.

docs.title: 1.2.1 FPGAs — Reconfigurable Hardware
docs.text:
A Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) is a chip that can be reconfigured. It contains hundreds of thousands of tiny logic blocks (called Look-Up Tables or LUTs), flip-flops, and programmable wiring. You describe what circuit you want in software, and the FPGA is configured to behave exactly like that circuit.

Key properties of FPGAs:

  • Reprogrammable — you can change the design in seconds.

  • Immediately available — buy one online for $30–$3000, plug it in.

  • Slower and more power-hungry than a custom chip for the same task.

  • Used for: prototyping, low-volume products, signal processing.

docs.title: 1.2.2 ASICs — Custom Silicon
docs.text:
An Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) is a chip that is permanently manufactured to implement one fixed design. Once manufactured, it cannot be changed.

Key properties of ASICs:

  • 10–100\(\times\) faster than an FPGA for the same circuit.

  • 10–100\(\times\) lower power consumption.

  • Costs millions of dollars to manufacture at commercial foundries.

  • Open-source foundries (Sky130, GF180) now offer free or very cheap tapeout slots — this tutorial uses those.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Digital Design Fundamentals
docs.text: Before writing a single line of hardware code, you need to understand how digital circuits work. This chapter builds the foundation from the ground up — no prior electronics knowledge is assumed.

docs.title: 2.1 Binary Numbers — Everything Is 0 or 1
docs.text:
A digital circuit deals exclusively with two voltage levels, which we call 0 (low, false, ground) and 1 (high, true, supply voltage). A group of \(n\) binary digits (bits) can represent \(2^n\) distinct values.

Table 2.1. Bit widths and their representable ranges Bits Number of values Example range 1 2 0 to 1 4 16 0 to 15 8 256 0 to 255 16 65,536 0 to 65,535 32 4.3 billion 0 to 4,294,967,295

Analogy: Binary as a Light Switch

A single bit is like a light switch — it is either ON (1) or OFF (0). A byte (8 bits) is like a row of 8 switches. The pattern 0100_0001 (reading left-to-right, most-significant to least-significant) represents the decimal number 65, which also happens to be the ASCII code for the letter ‘A’. Most of digital design is simply arranging and manipulating these switches with very precise timing.

docs.title: 2.2 Logic Gates — The Building Blocks
docs.text:
Logic gates are the simplest circuits. Each gate takes one or more binary inputs and produces one binary output.

Table 2.2. Basic logic gates Gate Symbol Behaviour NOT   A Flips the bit: 0->1, 1->0 AND A & B Output is 1 only if both inputs are 1 OR A | B Output is 1 if at least one input is 1 XOR A ^ B Output is 1 if inputs differ NAND  (A & B) NOT AND (universal gate) NOR  (A | B) NOT OR (universal gate)

Why NAND is Special

A NAND gate is called a universal gate because you can build any other logic gate using only NAND gates. This is why CMOS transistor-level logic is typically implemented as cascaded NAND/NOR pairs. In practice, standard cell libraries (like Sky130) provide hundreds of gate variants pre-characterised for area, power, and timing.

docs.title: 2.3 Combinational vs. Sequential Logic
docs.text: This is one of the most important distinctions in digital design:

docs.title: 2.3.1 Combinational Logic
docs.text:
The output depends only on the current inputs. There is no memory.

// A 4-bit adder --- pure combinational logic
module adder4 (
    input  logic [3:0] a, b,
    output logic [4:0] sum   // 5 bits to hold carry
);
    assign sum = a + b;      // No clock, no state
endmodule

Examples: adders, multiplexers, decoders, comparators.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Sequential Logic — The Flip-Flop
docs.text:
A flip-flop (FF) is a 1-bit memory element. It captures the value of its input (D) at the rising edge of a clock signal (CLK) and holds it until the next rising edge. This is the atom of state in digital design.

Figure 2.1. A D flip-flop samples its input D on every rising clock edge and holds the value on Q 
module dff (
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,   // active-low reset
    input  logic d,
    output logic q
);
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            q <= 1'b0;   // Reset to 0
        else
            q <= d;       // Sample D on rising clock edge
    end
endmodule

Active-Low Reset Explained

rst_n means “reset, active low”. The _n suffix is a hardware convention indicating the signal does its job when it equals 0 (not 1). So if (!rst_n) means “if reset is asserted”. This is because in CMOS circuits, pulling a signal low is faster and more reliable than driving it high.

docs.title: 2.4 Registers and Shift Registers
docs.text:
A group of flip-flops working together forms a register. A 32-bit register stores a 32-bit word. This is how a CPU stores the value in each of its general-purpose registers (e.g., x0–x31 in RISC-V).

module shift_reg_8 (
    input  logic clk, rst_n, shift_en,
    input  logic serial_in,
    output logic [7:0] parallel_out
);
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            parallel_out <= 8'h00;
        else if (shift_en)
            // Shift left, insert new bit at LSB
            parallel_out <= {parallel_out[6:0], serial_in};
    end
endmodule

This is exactly how the UART 16550 peripheral in this project receives serial data over a single wire — it shifts in one bit per baud period.

docs.title: 2.5 Finite State Machines
docs.text: A Finite State Machine (FSM) is a circuit that moves between a fixed set of named states, producing outputs and transitioning based on current state and inputs. Almost every non-trivial digital circuit contains at least one FSM.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Moore vs. Mealy
docs.text:
• Moore FSM: outputs depend only on the current state.

  • Mealy FSM: outputs depend on current state and inputs.

In practice most hardware FSMs use Moore style as it is easier to analyse timing.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Example: AXI-Lite Write Transaction FSM
docs.text:
The AXI4-Lite bus protocol (covered in Chapter 5) uses a 3-state FSM to manage write transactions:

Figure 2.2. Simplified AXI-Lite write FSM (from ip-library/processors/arm/cm0_ahblite_wrapper.sv) 
typedef enum logic [1:0] {
    IDLE, WRITE_ADDR, WRITE_DATA, WRITE_RESP
} state_t;

state_t state;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        state <= IDLE;
    else
        case (state)
            IDLE:       if (start_write) state <= WRITE_ADDR;
            WRITE_ADDR: if (addr_done)   state <= WRITE_DATA;
            WRITE_DATA: if (data_done)   state <= WRITE_RESP;
            WRITE_RESP: if (resp_rcvd)   state <= IDLE;
        endcase
end

docs.title: 2.6.1 Clock and Timing Budget
docs.text:
Every flip-flop in a design is driven by the same clock (or a derived clock). The time between two rising clock edges is called the clock period \(T_{clk}\). Inside this period, every bit of logic between two flip-flops must complete its computation. This constraint is called setup time:

\[T_{clk} \;\geq\; T_{setup} + T_{logic} + T_{clkskew}\]

where:

  • \(T_{setup}\) = flip-flop setup time (a few hundred picoseconds).

  • \(T_{logic}\) = propagation delay through combinational logic.

  • \(T_{clkskew}\) = difference in clock arrival time across chip.

The maximum operating frequency is:

\[f_{max} = \frac{1}{T_{clk,\min}}\]

A 100 MHz clock has a period of 10 ns. A 1 GHz clock has a period of 1 ns. The physical design tools (Chapter 9) automatically check that every combinational path meets timing — this is called Static Timing Analysis (STA).

docs.title: 2.6.2 Clock Domain Crossing
docs.text:
When two parts of a design run on different clocks, transferring data between them is dangerous — bits can be captured in a metastable state and produce random values. This is called a Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) problem, and it is one of the most common sources of silicon bugs.

CDC Danger Zone

Never connect a signal directly from one clock domain to another without a synchroniser circuit. At minimum, use a 2-flop synchroniser for single-bit signals and a gray-code pointer for multi-bit FIFOs (see ip-library/memory/async_fifo.core).

docs.title: 2.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Digital circuits use binary (0/1) signals.

  • Combinational logic computes outputs from current inputs (no memory).

  • Flip-flops store state and update on the clock edge.

  • FSMs manage complex sequencing behaviour.

  • Timing analysis ensures all computations complete within one clock period.

  • Clock Domain Crossing requires explicit synchronisation.

These fundamentals appear in every file in the rtl-templates/ and ip-library/ directories. In the next chapter we learn how to express these concepts in SystemVerilog — the language used throughout this project.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Hardware Description Languages
docs.text:
A Hardware Description Language (HDL) is a specialised programming language used to describe the structure and behaviour of electronic circuits. Unlike a normal programming language (Python, C++), an HDL describes hardware that exists physically in parallel — thousands of logic gates switching simultaneously, not one instruction at a time.

HDL is Not a Programming Language — It Is a Circuit Description

When you write a = b + c in Python, the computer executes that instruction once, sequentially. When you write the same in SystemVerilog as assign a = b + c;, you are describing a physical adder circuit that computes this value continuously, every nanosecond, in hardware. This parallel-by-default nature is the hardest mental shift for newcomers.

SystemVerilog is the industry-standard for custom chip design at companies like Intel, AMD, Qualcomm, and Apple. It is a superset of Verilog with stronger type checking, rich data types, and built-in assertion support.

docs.title: 3.2 The Module — SystemVerilog’s Basic Unit
docs.text:
Every hardware block is described as a module. Think of a module as a hardware component with labelled connectors (ports) on the outside and logic on the inside.

// Module declaration
module my_adder #(
    parameter int DATA_WIDTH = 8    // <-- Configurable parameter
) (
    // Port list --- the "connectors" on the outside
    input  logic                    clk,
    input  logic                    rst_n,
    input  logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0]   a,
    input  logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0]   b,
    output logic [DATA_WIDTH:0]     sum,   // 1 extra bit for carry
    output logic                    overflow
);

    // Internal signals (not visible outside)
    logic [DATA_WIDTH:0] sum_int;

    // Combinational logic
    assign sum_int  = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};
    assign overflow = sum_int[DATA_WIDTH];   // Carry out

    // Sequential logic --- register the output
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            sum <= '0;
        else
            sum <= sum_int;
    end

endmodule  // always end with the module name

docs.title: 3.2.1 Key Concepts in the Example
docs.text: parameter A compile-time constant. Change DATA_WIDTH to 16 and you instantly get a 16-bit adder — the same source code, different hardware. This is called parameterisation and it is how every reusable IP block in this project is written. logic The preferred signal type in SystemVerilog. It can hold 0, 1, X (unknown), or Z (high-impedance). Use logic everywhere; avoid the older wire/reg split. assign Describes continuous (combinational) logic. The right-hand side is always evaluated; the left-hand side updates instantly whenever any input changes. always_ff Describes flip-flop (sequential) logic. The _ff suffix makes the intent explicit to the synthesis tool and to human readers. ’0 SystemVerilog shorthand for a vector of all zeros, regardless of width. Similarly ’1 is all ones.

docs.title: 3.3 Real Example: The UART 16550 Transmitter
docs.text: The file rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv implements a full UART compatible with the classic 16550 chip. Let’s look at how it uses these concepts together.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Baud Rate Generator
docs.text:
// Baud rate generator --- divides system clock by (DLL + DLM*256)*16
logic [15:0] baud_div;   // Divisor from software register
logic [15:0] baud_cnt;   // Current count
logic        baud_tick;  // Pulses once per baud period

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        baud_cnt  <= 16'd0;
        baud_tick <= 1'b0;
    end else if (baud_cnt == baud_div - 1) begin
        baud_cnt  <= 16'd0;
        baud_tick <= 1'b1;   // Strobe for one clock cycle
    end else begin
        baud_cnt  <= baud_cnt + 16'd1;
        baud_tick <= 1'b0;
    end
end

How it works: If the system clock is 100 MHz and we want 115200 baud, we need to divide by \(\frac{100\,000\,000}{115200 \times 16} \approx 54\). Software writes 54 into the divisor register; the counter rolls over every 54 clocks, generating a baud_tick pulse.

docs.title: 3.3.2 TX Shift Register
docs.text:
typedef enum logic [2:0] {
    TX_IDLE, TX_START, TX_DATA, TX_STOP
} tx_state_t;
tx_state_t tx_state;

logic [7:0] tx_shift;  // Data being transmitted
logic [2:0] tx_bit;    // Bit counter (0-7)

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        tx_state <= TX_IDLE;
        uart_txd <= 1'b1;   // UART idle = line high
    end else if (baud_tick) begin
        case (tx_state)
            TX_IDLE:  if (tx_fifo_not_empty) begin
                          tx_shift <= tx_fifo_out;
                          uart_txd <= 1'b0;  // Start bit (low)
                          tx_state <= TX_DATA;
                          tx_bit   <= 3'd0;
                      end
            TX_DATA:  begin
                          uart_txd <= tx_shift[tx_bit];
                          if (tx_bit == 3'd7)
                              tx_state <= TX_STOP;
                          else
                              tx_bit <= tx_bit + 3'd1;
                      end
            TX_STOP:  begin
                          uart_txd <= 1'b1;  // Stop bit (high)
                          tx_state <= TX_IDLE;
                      end
        endcase
    end
end

This 20-line FSM is the heart of every UART in the world — a standard serialiser that converts a parallel byte into a serial bit stream.

docs.title: 3.4 The AXI4-Lite Slave Register File
docs.text:
The file rtl-templates/axi-bus/axi4_lite_slave.sv is one of the most important templates in the project. Almost every peripheral in the IP library uses it as its control register interface.

module axi4_lite_slave #(
    parameter int N_REGS    = 8,
    parameter int DATA_W    = 32,
    parameter int ADDR_W    = 5
) (
    input  logic                clk,
    input  logic                rst_n,
    // -- AXI4-Lite slave ports (36 signals total) --
    input  logic [ADDR_W-1:0]   s_axi_awaddr,
    input  logic                s_axi_awvalid,
    output logic                s_axi_awready,
    input  logic [DATA_W-1:0]   s_axi_wdata,
    input  logic [DATA_W/8-1:0] s_axi_wstrb,
    input  logic                s_axi_wvalid,
    output logic                s_axi_wready,
    output logic [1:0]          s_axi_bresp,
    output logic                s_axi_bvalid,
    input  logic                s_axi_bready,
    // ... (read port omitted for brevity)
    output logic [N_REGS*DATA_W-1:0] reg_out  // All register values
);
    logic [DATA_W-1:0] regs [0:N_REGS-1];

    // Write logic
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)
            foreach (regs[i]) regs[i] <= '0;
        else if (s_axi_awvalid && s_axi_awready &&
                 s_axi_wvalid  && s_axi_wready) begin
            // Word-addressed index from byte address
            automatic int idx = s_axi_awaddr[ADDR_W-1:2];
            for (int b = 0; b < DATA_W/8; b++)
                if (s_axi_wstrb[b])
                    regs[idx][b*8 +: 8] <= s_axi_wdata[b*8 +: 8];
        end
    end

    // Pack all registers onto output bus
    generate
        for (genvar i = 0; i < N_REGS; i++)
            assign reg_out[i*DATA_W +: DATA_W] = regs[i];
    endgenerate
endmodule

docs.title: 3.6 Generate Blocks — Hardware for Loops
docs.text:
A generate block creates hardware structures that repeat. Unlike a software loop (which runs N times), a generate loop creates N physical instances simultaneously.

generate
    for (genvar i = 0; i < N_TAPS; i++) begin : tap_gen
        // Creates N_TAPS independent multiply-accumulate units
        always_ff @(posedge clk)
            delay_line[i+1] <= delay_line[i];

        assign products[i] = delay_line[i] * coeff[i];
    end
endgenerate

This pattern appears in the FIR filter at rtl-templates/dsp/fir_filter.sv — the generate loop unrolls into N_TAPS parallel multiply-accumulate units.

docs.title: 3.7 Common Mistakes (and How to Avoid Them)
docs.text:
Table 3.3. Frequent SystemVerilog pitfalls Mistake Fix Mixing wire and reg Use logic everywhere Inferring latches with always_comb Cover all cases in if/case; add default Forgetting reset in always_ff Always add if (!rst_n) branch Using = (blocking) in always_ff Use <= (non-blocking) in clocked blocks Using <= in always_comb Use = (blocking) in combinational blocks Bit-width mismatch Use $bits() and explicit casts

Blocking vs Non-Blocking Assignment

  • a = b + 1; — blocking: executes immediately in sequence (use in always_comb).

  • a <= b + 1; — non-blocking: schedules update at end of time step (use in always_ff).

Mixing the two inside the same always_ff block causes subtle, hard-to-find simulation bugs.

docs.title: 3.8 Linting — Your First Quality Gate
docs.text:
Before simulation, always run the linter. This catches typos, width mismatches, and unconnected ports:

bash scripts/bash/lint_check.sh rtl-templates/

# Or directly with Verilator:
verilator --lint-only -Wall \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv

# Expected output for clean code:
# Linting: rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv ... PASS

docs.title: 3.9 Summary
docs.text:
• HDL describes hardware, not a sequence of instructions.

  • A module is the basic unit; ports are its interface.

  • assign = combinational; always_ff = sequential (clocked).

  • parameter makes modules reusable with different widths.

  • generate creates parallel hardware structures.

  • Always lint before simulating; always use non-blocking in always_ff.

With HDL fundamentals in hand, the next chapter dives into the most complex IP blocks in this project: processor cores.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Processor Cores
docs.text: A processor core is the engine of a System-on-Chip. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, executes them, and writes results back. This chapter explains processor architecture from scratch, then presents the open-source cores available in the ip-library/processors/ directory.

docs.title: 4.1 How a Processor Works — The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
docs.text:
Every processor, from the simplest microcontroller to Apple’s M3, repeats the same basic loop every clock cycle:

Figure 4.1. Classic 5-stage RISC pipeline Fetch (IF) The Program Counter (PC) register holds the address of the next instruction. The processor reads that address from instruction memory and increments PC by 4 (for 32-bit instructions). Decode (ID) The 32-bit instruction encoding is broken down into fields: opcode (what to do), source registers (rs1, rs2), destination register (rd), and immediate values. Execute (EX) The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs the actual computation: add, subtract, compare, shift, AND, OR, etc. Memory (MEM) Load instructions read data from RAM; store instructions write data to RAM. Jump/branch instructions check a condition and may redirect the PC. Write-Back (WB) The result is written into the destination register in the register file.

docs.title: 4.2 RISC-V — The Open Instruction Set
docs.text: RISC-V (pronounced “risk five”) is an open, free instruction set architecture (ISA) developed at UC Berkeley. Unlike ARM or x86, which are proprietary, anyone can implement a RISC-V processor without paying royalties. This has made it the dominant ISA in open-source chip design.

docs.title: 4.2.1 ISA Extensions
docs.text:
RISC-V is modular. The base ISA is called RV32I (32-bit, integer only). You add letters to enable optional extensions:

Table 4.1. Common RISC-V ISA extensions Letter Extension What it adds I Integer base 47 integer instructions (add, sub, load, store, branch) M Multiply/Divide MUL, MULH, DIV, REM instructions A Atomics Atomic read-modify-write (for multi-core locks) F Float (single) 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point D Double float 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point C Compressed 16-bit instructions (save code size by \(\sim\)25%)

Example: The CV32E40P core in this project implements RV32IMCFZicsr_Zifencei — 32-bit integer, multiply, compressed, single-precision float, plus two privilege-level extensions.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Register File
docs.text:
RISC-V has 32 general-purpose registers named x0–x31, each 32 bits wide (for RV32). Register x0 is hardwired to zero — reading it always returns 0, writing it does nothing. This is a deliberate design simplification that eliminates special-case instructions.

Table 4.2. RISC-V register file ABI conventions Register ABI Name Conventional Use x0 zero Always 0 (hardwired) x1 ra Return address x2 sp Stack pointer x5–x7, x28–x31 t0–t6 Temporaries (caller-saved) x8–x9, x18–x27 s0–s11 Saved registers (callee-saved) x10–x17 a0–a7 Function arguments / return values

docs.title: 4.2.3 Instruction Encoding
docs.text:
Every RISC-V instruction is exactly 32 bits (or 16 bits with the C extension). There are six instruction formats:

Figure 4.2. RISC-V instruction formats (32-bit words)

docs.title: 4.3 The Hand-Written RV32I Core
docs.text: The file rtl-templates/riscv-cores/rv32i_core.sv is a complete, working single-cycle RV32I processor written from scratch in \(\sim\)300 lines of SystemVerilog. Let’s walk through its key sections.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Fetch Stage
docs.text:
// Program Counter register
logic [31:0] pc;

// Combinational: next PC is either PC+4 or a branch target
logic [31:0] pc_next;
assign pc_next = branch_taken ? branch_target : pc + 32'd4;

// Sequential: update PC on every clock
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        pc <= RESET_ADDR;   // CPU starts executing from here
    else
        pc <= pc_next;
end

// Instruction memory read --- single-cycle (combinational)
assign instr = imem[pc[IMEM_AW+1:2]];  // Word-addressed

docs.title: 4.3.2 Decode Stage
docs.text:
// Unpack the 32-bit instruction into fields
logic [6:0]  opcode;
logic [4:0]  rs1, rs2, rd;
logic [2:0]  funct3;
logic [6:0]  funct7;
logic [31:0] imm_i, imm_s, imm_b;   // Sign-extended immediates

assign opcode = instr[6:0];
assign rd     = instr[11:7];
assign funct3 = instr[14:12];
assign rs1    = instr[19:15];
assign rs2    = instr[24:20];
assign funct7 = instr[31:25];

// I-type immediate: sign-extend bits [31:20]
assign imm_i  = {{20{instr[31]}}, instr[31:20]};

// B-type immediate: scrambled bit order by design (improves routing)
assign imm_b  = {{19{instr[31]}}, instr[31], instr[7],
                 instr[30:25], instr[11:8], 1'b0};

docs.title: 4.3.3 ALU
docs.text:
logic [31:0] alu_a, alu_b, alu_result;
logic [3:0]  alu_op;   // Decoded from opcode + funct3 + funct7

always_comb begin
    case (alu_op)
        ALU_ADD:  alu_result = alu_a + alu_b;
        ALU_SUB:  alu_result = alu_a - alu_b;
        ALU_AND:  alu_result = alu_a & alu_b;
        ALU_OR:   alu_result = alu_a | alu_b;
        ALU_XOR:  alu_result = alu_a ^ alu_b;
        ALU_SLL:  alu_result = alu_a << alu_b[4:0];   // Shift left logical
        ALU_SRL:  alu_result = alu_a >> alu_b[4:0];   // Shift right logical
        ALU_SRA:  alu_result = $signed(alu_a) >>> alu_b[4:0]; // Arithmetic shift
        ALU_SLT:  alu_result = ($signed(alu_a) < $signed(alu_b)) ? 32'd1 : 32'd0;
        ALU_SLTU: alu_result = (alu_a < alu_b) ? 32'd1 : 32'd0;
        default:  alu_result = 32'd0;
    endcase
end

docs.title: 4.5 PicoRV32 — The Arty A7 Workhorse
docs.text:
PicoRV32 (ip-library/processors/riscv/picorv32.core) is the recommended starting point for FPGA projects on the Arty A7 or KCU102. It is small, well-tested, and has a native AXI4-Lite master interface.

The wrapper file rtl-templates/riscv-cores/picorv32_wrapper.sv bridges the native PicoRV32 memory interface to AXI4-Lite:

// PicoRV32 native signals
logic        mem_valid;   // CPU wants a memory access
logic        mem_ready;   // Memory responds
logic [31:0] mem_addr;    // Address
logic [31:0] mem_wdata;   // Write data
logic [3:0]  mem_wstrb;   // Byte enables (0000 = read)
logic [31:0] mem_rdata;   // Read data back to CPU

// Bridge FSM: converts PicoRV32 native -> AXI4-Lite channels
typedef enum logic [1:0] { BR_IDLE, BR_WRITE, BR_READ } br_state_t;
br_state_t br_state;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        br_state <= BR_IDLE;
        mem_ready <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
        mem_ready <= 1'b0;
        case (br_state)
            BR_IDLE: if (mem_valid) begin
                if (|mem_wstrb) begin      // Write if any strobe set
                    m_axi_awaddr  <= mem_addr;
                    m_axi_awvalid <= 1'b1;
                    m_axi_wdata   <= mem_wdata;
                    m_axi_wstrb   <= mem_wstrb;
                    m_axi_wvalid  <= 1'b1;
                    br_state      <= BR_WRITE;
                end else begin             // Otherwise read
                    m_axi_araddr  <= mem_addr;
                    m_axi_arvalid <= 1'b1;
                    br_state      <= BR_READ;
                end
            end
            // ... (write/read completion states)
        endcase
    end
end

docs.text:

The wrapper ip-library/processors/arm/cm0_ahblite_wrapper.sv converts the Cortex-M0’s AHB-Lite bus to AXI4-Lite:

docs.text:
The pipeline/templates/soc_spec_template.yaml file describes how to assemble a complete SoC from these components:

cpu:

memory_map:
  - { name: boot_rom, base: 0x00000000, size: 0x10000, type: rom  }
  - { name: sram,     base: 0x20000000, size: 0x40000, type: sram }
