docs.title: 4.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Every processor runs a Fetch -> Decode -> Execute -> Memory -> Write-Back cycle.

  • RISC-V is the open, royalty-free ISA used in most open-source chip designs.

  • The project provides cores from ultra-tiny (SERV, \(<\)2kGE) to high-performance (CVA6, Linux-capable).

  • The hand-written rv32i_core.sv is a teaching tool; for real projects use PicoRV32, CV32E40P, or Ibex.

  • Cores connect to peripherals through bus protocols — the topic of the next chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Bus Protocols and Interconnects
docs.text:
A bus protocol is a set of rules that defines how two hardware blocks communicate — who drives which signal, how they handshake, and what happens when one is slower than the other. Getting this right is critical: every IP block in this project communicates through a bus.

Analogy: Bus Protocol as a Phone Call Convention

Imagine two people agreeing on a calling protocol: “I say your name, you say ‘ready’, I deliver my message, you say ‘received’, then we hang up.” AXI4 works similarly, but with hardware signals instead of words. Both sides must follow the protocol exactly — one wrong signal and the communication hangs forever.

docs.title: 5.1 Overview of Bus Protocols Used in This Project
docs.text: Table 5.1. Bus protocols and their typical use cases Protocol Origin Channels Best Used For AXI4 ARM (AMBA 4) 5 channels High-bandwidth DRAM & DMA AXI4-Lite ARM (AMBA 4) 5 channels CSR registers, simple peripherals AXI4-Stream ARM (AMBA 4) 1 channel Streaming data (video, DSP, DMA) APB3/4 ARM (AMBA 3/4) 1 channel Low-power slow peripherals Wishbone B4 OpenCores 1 channel Simple open-source designs TileLink UC Berkeley 5 channels RISC-V ecosystem (Rocket, BOOM)

docs.title: 5.2 AXI4-Lite — The Register Access Bus
docs.text: AXI4-Lite is the simplest of the AXI family. It is used for accessing configuration and status registers (CSRs) in peripherals. Every peripheral in the IP library (UART, SPI, I2C, FIR filter, etc.) exposes its registers through an AXI4-Lite slave port.

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Five Channels
docs.text:
AXI4-Lite has five independent channels, each with a valid/ready handshake. The master (e.g., the CPU) initiates transactions. The slave (e.g., the UART peripheral) responds.

Figure 5.1. AXI4-Lite channel structure — M to S (blue), S to M (green)

docs.title: 5.2.2 The Valid/Ready Handshake
docs.text:
The most important concept in AXI is the valid/ready handshake. A transfer occurs only when both VALID and READY are high on the same clock edge:

Figure 5.2. AXI handshake: transfer occurs when VALID AND READY are both 1

Key Handshake Rule

The master asserts VALID when it has data ready. The slave asserts READY when it can accept data. The master must not deassert VALID once asserted (until the transfer completes). The slave can deassert READY at any time. This asymmetry is by design.

docs.title: 5.2.3 A Complete AXI4-Lite Write Transaction
docs.text:
task axil_write(input [3:0] addr, input [31:0] data);
    @(posedge clk);
    // Assert write address channel
    s_axi_awaddr  <= addr;
    s_axi_awvalid <= 1'b1;
    // Assert write data channel simultaneously
    s_axi_wdata   <= data;
    s_axi_wstrb   <= 4'hF;    // All byte enables active
    s_axi_wvalid  <= 1'b1;
    // Ready to accept write response
    s_axi_bready  <= 1'b1;

    // Wait until slave accepts address AND data
    wait(s_axi_awready && s_axi_wready);
    @(posedge clk);
    s_axi_awvalid <= 1'b0;
    s_axi_wvalid  <= 1'b0;

    // Wait for write response (BRESP)
    wait(s_axi_bvalid);
    @(posedge clk);
    s_axi_bready <= 1'b0;
endtask

docs.title: 5.2.4 BRESP and RRESP — Response Codes
docs.text:
After every write, the slave sends a 2-bit response code:

Table 5.2. AXI BRESP / RRESP codes Code Meaning When to see it 2’b00 OKAY Normal successful transaction 2’b01 EXOKAY Exclusive access OK (not used in AXI4-Lite) 2’b10 SLVERR Slave error (address not mapped) 2’b11 DECERR Decode error (address not decoded)

docs.title: 5.3 AXI4-Stream — The Data Pipeline Bus
docs.text:
AXI4-Stream is used for high-speed, point-to-point data flow where there are no addresses — just a continuous stream of data words. It is used for:

  • DSP pipelines: ADC samples -> FIR filter -> FFT -> output

  • Video: pixel data from image sensor -> processing -> display

  • DMA data movement: memory -> network DMA engine -> Ethernet

// AXI4-Stream Slave Input
input  logic                    s_axis_tvalid,  // Data valid
output logic                    s_axis_tready,  // Can accept data
input  logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0]   s_axis_tdata,   // The data
input  logic                    s_axis_tlast,   // Last in packet
input  logic [DATA_WIDTH/8-1:0] s_axis_tkeep,   // Byte enables

// AXI4-Stream Master Output
output logic                    m_axis_tvalid,
input  logic                    m_axis_tready,
output logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0]   m_axis_tdata,
output logic                    m_axis_tlast

The FIR filter in rtl-templates/dsp/fir_filter.sv has AXI4-Stream on both its input (sample in) and output (filtered sample out):

fir_filter #(
    .N_TAPS(32),
    .DATA_WIDTH(16),
    .COEFF_WIDTH(16),
    .SYMMETRIC(1)
) u_fir (
    .clk          (clk),
    .rst_n        (rst_n),
    // Input: raw ADC samples
    .s_axis_tdata (adc_data),
    .s_axis_tvalid(adc_valid),
    .s_axis_tready(adc_ready),
    .s_axis_tlast (1'b0),     // Continuous stream, no packets
    // Output: filtered samples
    .m_axis_tdata (fir_out),
    .m_axis_tvalid(fir_valid),
    .m_axis_tready(fft_ready)
);

docs.title: 5.4 Wishbone B4 — The Open-Source Classic
docs.text:
Wishbone is the bus used by the OpenCores community and the Caravel Harness (Efabless MPW tapeout infrastructure). It has a simpler, single-channel interface compared to AXI:

// Wishbone Master outputs / Slave inputs
output logic        wb_cyc_o,   // Bus cycle in progress
output logic        wb_stb_o,   // Strobe (this cycle is for this slave)
output logic        wb_we_o,    // Write enable
output logic [31:0] wb_adr_o,   // Address
output logic [31:0] wb_dat_o,   // Write data
output logic [3:0]  wb_sel_o,   // Byte select

// Wishbone Slave outputs / Master inputs
input  logic        wb_ack_i,   // Acknowledge (transfer complete)
input  logic        wb_err_i,   // Error
input  logic [31:0] wb_dat_i    // Read data

A Wishbone transfer completes in one cycle when CYC & STB & ACK are all 1. The ao486 x86 core uses Wishbone as its native bus (see ip-library/processors/x86/ao486_wb_wrapper.sv).

docs.title: 5.5 APB — Advanced Peripheral Bus
docs.text:
APB is the simplest AMBA bus. It has a 2-cycle minimum transaction and is designed for low-power, low-speed peripherals. SoCs typically use APB for slow devices like RTC, watchdog timers, and GPIO controllers, connected to the AXI fabric through an APB bridge.

input  logic        pclk,      // Clock
input  logic        presetn,   // Reset
input  logic [31:0] paddr,     // Address (from master)
input  logic        psel,      // Select this slave
input  logic        penable,   // Enable (2nd cycle)
input  logic        pwrite,    // Write (1) / Read (0)
input  logic [31:0] pwdata,    // Write data
output logic [31:0] prdata,    // Read data (from slave)
output logic        pready,    // Slave ready
output logic        pslverr    // Slave error

docs.title: 5.6 The Crossbar Interconnect
docs.text:
When multiple masters (e.g., CPU + DMA) need to access multiple slaves (e.g., SRAM + UART + SPI), a crossbar is needed. The project provides ip-library/bus/axi4_lite_crossbar.core:

Figure 5.3. AXI4-Lite crossbar connecting CPU and DMA to four slave peripherals

docs.title: 5.7 Register Maps — How Software Talks to Hardware
docs.text:
Every peripheral exposes its internal state through registers mapped at fixed addresses. Software (running on the CPU) reads and writes these addresses to control the hardware. The register map is the most important interface document for any IP block.

Table 5.3. Example register map for UART 16550 (simplified) Offset Name Access Reset Description 0x00 CTRL RW 0x0000 Control: bit 0=enable, bit 1=loopback 0x04 STATUS RO 0x0060 Status: bit 0=busy, bits 6:5=TX empty 0x08 BAUD RW 0x0036 Baud divisor (default = 54 -> 115200) 0x0C DATA RW — Write=TX FIFO, Read=RX FIFO 0x10 IRQ_EN RW 0x0000 Interrupt enables, bit per source

These register maps are generated automatically from YAML specifications using scripts/python/regmap_gen.py (covered in Chapter 11).

docs.title: 5.8 Formal Properties for Bus Protocols
docs.text:
The file verification/formal/uart/uart_axil_props.sv contains assertions that mathematically prove the AXI4-Lite interface is implemented correctly. For example:

// Once the master asserts AWVALID, it must hold it
// until the slave asserts AWREADY (handshake rule)
property awvalid_stable;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (s_axi_awvalid && !s_axi_awready) |=>
    s_axi_awvalid;  // Must still be valid next cycle
endproperty

assert property (awvalid_stable)
    else $error("AWVALID violated: deasserted before AWREADY");

This is not a simulation test — it is a formal mathematical proof that covers all possible input sequences. We discuss formal verification fully in Chapter 7.

docs.title: 5.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Every IP block communicates through a bus protocol with defined signals and handshakes.

  • AXI4-Lite: 5-channel, valid/ready handshake, for control registers.

  • AXI4-Stream: streaming data with no addresses.

  • Wishbone: simple, open-source, used by Caravel/Efabless tapeout.

  • APB: slowest and simplest, for low-power peripherals.

  • A crossbar connects multiple masters to multiple slaves.

  • Register maps define how software controls hardware.

docs.title: Chapter 6: FPGA Prototyping
docs.text: FPGA prototyping is the critical halfway point between writing RTL on your laptop and shipping silicon to a foundry. You program your design onto a real FPGA board, verify it works in hardware at speed, and fix any bugs before committing millions of dollars to manufacture.

docs.title: 6.1 How an FPGA Works Internally
docs.text:
An FPGA chip is a sea of programmable resources:

Figure 6.1. Internal structure of an FPGA (simplified) CLB (Configurable Logic Block) Contains 4–8 Look-Up Tables (LUTs) and flip-flops. A 6-input LUT can implement any Boolean function of 6 variables. After synthesis, your HDL logic is mapped onto these LUTs. BRAM (Block RAM) Hard-macro memory blocks (18 Kb or 36 Kb each). Used for FIFOs, instruction memory, coefficient tables. Much more efficient than building memories from LUTs. DSP48/DSP58 Slice Dedicated 18\(\times\)18 multiplier+accumulator. The FIR filter maps each tap’s multiply-add onto one DSP slice. I/O Banks Configurable I/O pins supporting LVCMOS, LVDS differential, DDR4 memory interface (via SERDES), and high-speed serial (PCIe, GTH). PLL/MMCM Clock management tiles — generate phase-locked, divided, or multiplied clocks from the board oscillator.

docs.title: 6.2 The Xilinx Vivado Flow
docs.text: Vivado is Xilinx’s primary EDA suite for Artix-7, Kintex UltraScale+, and Zynq devices. The project uses a non-project (scripted) mode — entirely driven by Tcl scripts, which is reproducible and version-control friendly.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Build Flow Overview
docs.text: Figure 6.2. Vivado non-project build flow

docs.title: 6.2.2 Running the Arty A7 Build
docs.text:
# Build bitstream (takes 5-20 minutes depending on design size)
vivado -mode batch \
    -source fpga/xilinx-artix7/build_arty_a7.tcl \
    -tclargs top 4   # top module name, 4 parallel jobs

# Output:
#   fpga/xilinx-artix7/output/top.bit
#   fpga/xilinx-artix7/output/top_timing.rpt   (timing report)
#   fpga/xilinx-artix7/output/top_util.rpt     (resource usage)

# Program the FPGA (board must be connected via USB-JTAG)
vivado -mode batch \
    -source fpga/xilinx-artix7/program_arty.tcl \
    -tclargs fpga/xilinx-artix7/output/top.bit

docs.title: 6.2.3 Reading Timing Reports
docs.text:
After synthesis, always check the timing report. A negative Worst Negative Slack (WNS) means timing is violated — the design will malfunction at the target clock frequency:

# From top_timing.rpt:
# Design Timing Summary
# ---------------------
# WNS (ns)   TNS (ns)   TNS Failing Endpoints
#   2.134      0.000        0              <- PASS: WNS positive
#
# If failing:
# WNS (ns)   TNS (ns)   TNS Failing Endpoints
#  -0.512    -12.340       47             <- FAIL: must fix

What to Do When Timing Fails

  1. Reduce clock frequency: In the XDC file, change the clock period from 10 ns (100 MHz) to 12 ns (83 MHz).

  2. Pipeline the critical path: Add a register stage to break long logic chains into shorter ones.

  3. Try aggressive optimisation: Use -directive AggressiveExplore in place/route commands.

  4. Restructure the logic: Reduce logic depth between flip-flops.

docs.title: 6.3 Constraint Files (XDC)
docs.text:
A constraint file (.xdc) tells Vivado three things:

  1. Which physical pin carries which port signal.

  2. What the clock frequency is.

  3. Any exceptions to the timing rules (false paths, multicycle paths).

docs.title: 6.3.1 Clock Constraint
docs.text:
# Tell Vivado: the signal sys_clk comes in on pin E3, at 100 MHz
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN E3 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } \
    [get_ports { sys_clk }]

create_clock -add -name sys_clk_pin \
    -period 10.00 \          # 10 ns = 100 MHz
    -waveform {0 5} \        # rises at 0 ns, falls at 5 ns
    [get_ports { sys_clk }]

docs.title: 6.3.2 I/O Pin Constraint
docs.text:
# LEDs (4 green LEDs on the board)
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN H5  IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { led[0] }]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN J5  IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { led[1] }]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN T9  IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { led[2] }]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN T10 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { led[3] }]

# UART (connects to on-board FT2232HQ USB-UART bridge)
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN D10 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { uart_txd }]
set_property -dict { PACKAGE_PIN A9  IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 } [get_ports { uart_rxd }]

Package pin names (like E3, H5) come from the board’s schematic and the FPGA’s pinout diagram. The complete files for all boards are in fpga/constraints/.

docs.title: 6.4 Resource Utilisation — What Fits Where
docs.text:
After synthesis, check the utilisation report to understand how much of the FPGA is used:

Table 6.1. Typical utilisation for a UART+SPI+I2C peripheral SoC on Arty A7-35T Resource Used Available % Notes LUT 3,124 20,800 15.0% OK Flip-Flops 2,012 41,600 4.8% OK BRAM (18K) 8 50 16.0% OK DSP48 0 90 0% No multipliers used I/O 12 210 5.7% OK

Utilisation Guidelines

  • Stay below 70% LUT utilisation to allow Vivado’s router room to manoeuvre. Above 80% causes dramatically longer build times and timing failures.

  • BRAM and DSP can safely use up to 90% since they don’t affect routing congestion.

  • If your design uses \(>\)70% LUTs on an Arty A7-35T, consider moving to the A7-100T (same board, larger chip).

docs.title: 6.5 Intel Quartus Flow (DE10-Nano)
docs.text:
The DE10-Nano uses an Intel Cyclone V SoC FPGA. The tool is Quartus Prime. The project provides fpga/intel-altera/de10_nano_quartus.tcl:

# Build from command line:
quartus_sh --script fpga/intel-altera/de10_nano_quartus.tcl

# Program via JTAG:
quartus_pgm -m jtag \
    -o "p;fpga/intel-altera/output/de10_nano_top.sof"

Key differences from Vivado:

  • Timing constraints use SDC files (de10_nano.sdc).

  • Resource primitives are called ALMs (Adaptive Logic Modules) instead of LUTs.

  • The HPS (Hard Processor System) on the Cyclone V SoC can run Linux and talk to the FPGA fabric via a lightweight AXI bus.

docs.title: 6.6 ILA — In-Circuit Debugging
docs.text:
When a bug only appears on real hardware (not in simulation), you need Integrated Logic Analyser (ILA) — a logic analyser baked into your FPGA design:

source fpga/ip-cores/clk_wizard_config.tcl

# Create ILA with 4 probes, 1024 sample depth
create_ila ila_debug 4 1024

(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic uart_txd;
(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic [7:0] tx_data;
(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic tx_valid;

The ( mark_debug ) attribute tells Vivado to route these signals to the ILA probe inputs. After programming the FPGA:

# 1. Open Hardware Manager in Vivado GUI
# 2. Program device with both .bit and .ltx files:
vivado -mode batch \
    -source fpga/xilinx-ultrascale-plus/program_kcu.tcl \
    -tclargs output/top.bit output/top.ltx

# 3. In Vivado Hardware Manager:
#    - Set trigger: uart_txd = 0 (start bit falling edge)
#    - Arm the trigger
#    - Send data from terminal
#    - View captured waveform

docs.title: 6.7 FPGA-in-the-Loop Testing
docs.text:
After programming the FPGA, the script verification/fpga-proto/ fpga_in_the_loop.py exercises the hardware from a Python test script running on your laptop:

from verification.fpga_proto.fpga_in_the_loop import FPGAInterface, UARTLoopbackTest

# Connect to FPGA via UART
fpga = FPGAInterface(port='/dev/ttyUSB0', baud=115200)
fpga.connect()

# Run UART register walk and loopback test
test = UARTLoopbackTest(fpga, uart_base=0x40000000)
fails = test.run_all()
# Output:
#   PASS: [Scratch] addr=0x001C got=0xDEADBEEF exp=0xDEADBEEF
#   PASS: [LSR.DR set] addr=0x0014 got=0x00000001 exp=0x00000001
#   Result: PASS (0 failures)

docs.title: 6.8 Summary
docs.text:
• FPGAs are reconfigurable chips made of LUTs, flip-flops, BRAM, and DSP slices connected by programmable routing.

  • The Vivado/Quartus flow takes RTL -> synthesis -> place & route -> bitstream -> JTAG programming.

  • Constraint files (.xdc) define pin assignments and clock frequencies.

  • WNS \(\geq\) 0 means timing passes; negative WNS means the design will malfunction at that clock frequency.

  • ILA cores allow capturing internal signals on real hardware without oscilloscopes.

  • FPGA-in-the-loop scripts automate hardware testing from Python.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Verification
docs.text:
The Golden Rule of Chip Design

“A chip bug found in simulation costs one hour to fix. The same bug found after tapeout costs three months and millions of dollars to re-spin.”

Verification is not optional. In the semiconductor industry, 60–80% of engineering effort goes into verification, not design. This chapter shows you the three major verification techniques used in this project.

docs.title: 7.1 Three Verification Approaches
docs.text: Table 7.1. Verification methods and tools Method Tool What It Proves Simulation (directed) Icarus, Questa, Verilator RTL matches testbench expectations Simulation (random/UVM) Questa + UVM Broad coverage of corner cases Formal verification SymbiYosys Mathematical proof for all inputs

docs.title: 7.2 Simulation — Running Your RTL Like a Program
docs.text: A simulator executes your HDL code, propagating signal changes through time according to the clock. You write a testbench that provides stimulus (inputs) and checks responses (outputs).

docs.title: 7.2.1 Quick Simulation with Icarus Verilog
docs.text:
Icarus Verilog (iverilog) is free, fast to compile, and supports SystemVerilog. It is the go-to tool for quick functional checks:

# Method 1: Use the convenience script
bash scripts/bash/sim_run.sh \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv \
    verification/tb-templates/uart_16550_tb.sv \
    tb icarus

# Method 2: Manual compile and run
iverilog -g2012 \
    -o sim_output/sim_uart \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv \
    verification/tb-templates/uart_16550_tb.sv

./sim_output/sim_uart

# View waveform
gtkwave sim_output/dump.vcd

docs.title: 7.2.2 Anatomy of the UART Testbench
docs.text:
The file verification/tb-templates/uart_16550_tb.sv exercises the UART. Let’s look at the key patterns:

module uart_16550_tb;

    // 1. Declare signals to drive the DUT
    logic clk, rst_n;
    logic [3:0] s_axi_awaddr;
    logic [31:0] s_axi_wdata;
    // ... (all AXI signals)

    // 2. Loopback TX->RX for self-test
    assign uart_rxd = uart_txd;

    // 3. Instantiate the Device Under Test (DUT)
    uart_16550 #(
        .CLOCK_FREQ_HZ(100_000_000)
    ) dut (
        .clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n),
        .uart_txd(uart_txd), .uart_rxd(uart_rxd)
        // ... connect all ports
    );

    // 4. Generate clock: toggle every 5 ns = 100 MHz
    initial clk = 0;
    always #5 clk = ~clk;

    // 5. Reusable tasks (AXI register read/write)
    task axil_write(input [3:0] addr, input [31:0] data);
        // ... (drives AXI signals, shown in Chapter 5)
    endtask

    // 6. Main test sequence
    initial begin
        rst_n = 0;
        repeat(5) @(posedge clk);
        rst_n = 1;

        // Test: TX loopback --- send 'A', expect to receive 'A'
        axil_write(MCR, 32'h10);      // Enable loopback
        axil_write(RBR, 32'h41);      // Send 'A' (0x41)
        repeat(2000) @(posedge clk);  // Wait for serial TX

        axil_read(LSR, rd_data);
        check("RX data ready", rd_data[0] == 1'b1);
        axil_read(RBR, rd_data);
        check("Got 'A'", rd_data[7:0] == 8'h41);

        $display("RESULT:
        $finish;
    end

    // 7. Simulation timeout guard
    initial begin
        #5_000_000; $display("TIMEOUT"); $finish;
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 7.2.3 Verilator — Fast C++ Simulation
docs.text:
For large designs, Icarus is too slow. Verilator compiles SystemVerilog into C++ and then compiles that with GCC, producing simulations that run 10–100\(\times\) faster. It also performs the most thorough lint checking of any open-source tool.

# Lint only (very fast, catches many errors)
verilator --lint-only -Wall \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv

# Build a simulation binary
verilator --binary --trace -Wall \
    --top-module uart_16550 \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv \
    eda/verilator/sim_top.cpp \
    -o sim_output/Vuart_16550

# Run and view waveform
./sim_output/Vuart_16550 --trace
gtkwave sim_trace.vcd

docs.title: 7.3 cocotb — Python-Driven Verification
docs.text: cocotb allows you to write testbenches in Python instead of SystemVerilog. This is ideal when you have existing Python test vectors, when the test logic is complex (file I/O, mathematical comparison), or when you prefer Python’s rich library ecosystem.

docs.title: 7.3.1 How cocotb Works
docs.text: Figure 7.1. cocotb architecture: Python controls the HDL simulator

docs.title: 7.3.2 cocotb UART Test
docs.text:
The complete test is at verification/cocotb/uart_test/test_uart_16550.py:

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import RisingEdge, Timer
from cocotb_bus.drivers.amba import AXI4LiteMaster

@cocotb.test()
async def test_uart_loopback(dut):
    """Test: send byte over UART, receive it back via loopback."""

    # Start the 100 MHz clock
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk, 10, units="ns").start())

    # Reset
    dut.rst_n.value = 0
    await Timer(50, units="ns")
    dut.rst_n.value = 1
    await Timer(100, units="ns")

    # Create AXI4-Lite master driver
    axil = AXI4LiteMaster(dut, "s_axi", dut.clk)

    # Set DLAB=1, program baud divisor to 54 (115200 @ 100MHz)
    await axil.write(0x0C, 0x80)   # LCR: DLAB=1
    await axil.write(0x00, 54)     # DLL = 54
    await axil.write(0x04, 0)      # DLM = 0
    await axil.write(0x0C, 0x03)   # LCR: 8N1, DLAB=0

    # Enable loopback, send 'A' (0x41)
    await axil.write(0x10, 0x10)   # MCR: loopback bit
    await axil.write(0x00, 0x41)   # THR: send 'A'

    # Wait for UART to transmit (~2000 bit periods at 115200 baud)
    await Timer(2000 * 10, units="ns")

    # Check Line Status Register --- Data Ready bit should be set
    lsr = await axil.read(0x14)
    assert lsr & 0x01, f"LSR.DR not set: 0x{lsr:08X}"

    # Read received byte
    rxd = await axil.read(0x00)
    assert rxd & 0xFF == 0x41, f"Expected 'A' (0x41), got 0x{rxd:02X}"
    dut._log.info("PASS: UART loopback received 'A'")

cd verification/cocotb/uart_test

# With Icarus
make SIM=icarus

# With Verilator
make SIM=verilator

# With Questa (if installed)
make SIM=questa

docs.title: 7.4 Formal Verification — Mathematical Proof
docs.text: Simulation shows the design works for the test vectors you thought of. Formal verification proves the design works for every possible input sequence — including inputs you didn’t think of.

docs.title: 7.4.1 How Formal Verification Works
docs.text:
A formal tool (like SymbiYosys) converts your RTL and properties into a mathematical satisfiability problem (SAT/SMT). It then searches for a counter-example — an input sequence that violates your property. If it finds none after exploring all reachable states, the property is proven.

Figure 7.2. Formal verification flow using SymbiYosys

docs.title: 7.4.2 SVA — SystemVerilog Assertions
docs.text:
Properties are written as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA). The file verification/formal/uart/uart_axil_props.sv contains:

// Property 1: AWVALID must remain stable until AWREADY
// (AXI handshake protocol rule)
property awvalid_stays_high;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (s_axi_awvalid && !s_axi_awready) |=>  s_axi_awvalid;
endproperty
assert property (awvalid_stays_high);

// Property 2: BRESP must always be OKAY or SLVERR (never undefined)
property bresp_valid;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    s_axi_bvalid |-> (s_axi_bresp inside {2'b00, 2'b10});
endproperty
assert property (bresp_valid);

// Cover point: prove it IS possible to complete a write transaction
property write_completes;
    @(posedge clk)
    s_axi_awvalid |-> ##[1:20] s_axi_bvalid;
endproperty
cover property (write_completes);

docs.title: 7.4.3 SymbiYosys Configuration File
docs.text:
[options]
mode bmc        # Bounded Model Check (try to find counterexample)
depth 20        # Search up to 20 clock cycles deep

[engines]
smtbmc          # Use SMT-based model checker

[script]
read -sv rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv
read -sv verification/formal/uart/uart_axil_props.sv
prep -top uart_16550

[files]
rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv
verification/formal/uart/uart_axil_props.sv

sby -f verification/formal/uart/uart_props.sby

# Output (if all properties pass):
# [SBY] engine_0: Status returned by engine: PASS
# [SBY] summary: Elapsed clock time [H:MM:SS]: 0:00:12
# [SBY] DONE (PASS, rc=0)

What “PASS” Means in Formal Verification

When SymbiYosys says PASS with depth = 20, it means: “For every possible reset state and every possible sequence of inputs over 20 clock cycles, this property cannot be violated.” This is significantly stronger than any simulation test — it covers an effectively infinite number of input sequences.

docs.title: 7.5 UVM — Universal Verification Methodology
docs.text:
For large, complex SoCs, engineers use UVM — a standardised class library (IEEE 1800.2) for building reusable, structured testbenches. UVM provides:

  • Agents: encapsulate a protocol driver + monitor.

  • Sequences: describe streams of transactions.

  • Scoreboards: automatically compare expected vs. actual.

  • Coverage: measure what percentage of functionality was tested.

The project provides a complete UVM environment template at verification/uvm/uart_uvm_env.sv:

class uart_env extends uvm_env;
    `uvm_component_utils(uart_env)

    axil_agent      agent;       // Drives + monitors AXI4-Lite
    uart_scoreboard scoreboard;  // Checks outputs are correct

    function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
        agent      = axil_agent::type_id::create("agent", this);
        scoreboard = uart_scoreboard::type_id::create("scoreboard", this);
    endfunction

    function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
        // Connect monitor output to scoreboard input
        agent.monitor.ap.connect(scoreboard.imp);
    endfunction
endclass

class reg_walk_seq extends uvm_sequence #(axil_transaction);
    task body();
        reg_write_seq wr;
        for (int i = 0; i < n_regs; i++) begin
            wr = reg_write_seq::type_id::create("wr");
            wr.addr = i * 4;
            wr.data = $urandom();  // Random data per register
            wr.start(m_sequencer);
        end
    endtask
endclass

docs.title: 7.6 Functional Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage measures what fraction of the design’s functionality has been exercised. Without coverage, you cannot know whether your tests are complete:

covergroup uart_cg @(posedge clk);
    cp_word_len: coverpoint lcr[1:0] {
        bins five_bit  = {2'b00};
        bins six_bit   = {2'b01};
        bins seven_bit = {2'b10};
        bins eight_bit = {2'b11};  // Most common
    }
    cp_parity: coverpoint lcr[3] {
        bins no_parity  = {0};
        bins has_parity = {1};
    }
    // Cross: test every word-length $\times$ parity combination
    cx_mode: cross cp_word_len, cp_parity;
endgroup

Industry practice is to target 95–100% functional coverage before signing off on a design.

docs.title: 7.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Directed simulation (Icarus/Verilator) is fast for early debugging of specific functionality.

  • cocotb lets you write testbenches in Python for powerful, flexible verification with real-world data.

  • Formal verification (SymbiYosys + SVA) mathematically proves properties hold for all possible inputs.

  • UVM provides a scalable framework for large SoC verification with reusable agents, sequences, and scoreboards.

  • Functional coverage measures whether your tests are complete.

  • A bug found in verification costs hours; found in silicon costs months.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Synthesis
docs.text:
Synthesis is the translation of your RTL (register-transfer level) description into a gate-level netlist — a list of primitive logic gates, flip-flops, and multiplexers connected by wires, taken from a technology library.

Analogy: Synthesis is Like a Compiler

Just as a C compiler turns your source code into machine instructions for a specific CPU, a synthesis tool turns your SystemVerilog into logic gates for a specific technology (FPGA LUTs or ASIC standard cells). The synthesis tool is smarter than a compiler: it re-arranges, shares, and optimises logic to meet your timing and area targets.

docs.title: 8.1 What Happens During Synthesis
docs.text:
Synthesis consists of three main steps:

Figure 8.1. Three steps of RTL synthesis Elaboration The tool reads your SystemVerilog, resolves parameters, expands generate blocks, and builds an internal representation (a network of boolean functions). Technology Mapping The tool maps each boolean function to available primitives: LUTs for FPGAs, or standard cells (NAND2, DFF, MUX) for ASICs. This step reads the liberty file (.lib) which describes every cell’s function, timing, and power. Optimisation The tool applies algebraic transformations, logic sharing, retiming (moving registers to shorten critical paths), and constant propagation to meet timing targets while minimising area and power.

docs.title: 8.2 Yosys — Open-Source Synthesis
docs.text: Yosys is the primary open-source synthesis tool, used for both FPGA and ASIC flows. It supports SystemVerilog (via the read_verilog -sv command) and has backends for Sky130, GF180, and generic gates.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Sky130 Synthesis Script
docs.text:
The file eda/yosys/synth_sky130.ys synthesises a design for Sky130A:

# Read the design
read_verilog -sv rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv

# Set the top-level module
hierarchy -check -top uart_16550

# Generic synthesis passes
proc        # Convert always blocks to logic
flatten     # Inline all module hierarchy
tribuf      # Handle tri-state buffers
opt_clean   # Remove unused cells and signals
opt         # Boolean optimisation
fsm         # FSM optimisation (encode states better)
opt         # Optimise again after FSM changes
memory      # Infer memories (SRAMs, FIFOs)
opt_clean

# Technology mapping
# Step 1: Map flip-flops to Sky130 DFF cells
dfflibmap -liberty $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.ref/sky130_fd_sc_hd/lib/\
    sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib

# Step 2: Map logic to Sky130 standard cells via ABC
abc -liberty $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.ref/sky130_fd_sc_hd/lib/\
    sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib \
    -constr eda/yosys/sky130_abc.constr

# Final cleanup
opt_clean
clean

# Write outputs
write_verilog -noattr gdsii/outputs/uart_16550_netlist.v
stat            # Print area statistics

docs.title: 8.2.2 Running Yosys
docs.text:
# Generic synthesis (technology-independent, good for quick checks)
bash scripts/bash/synth_yosys.sh uart_16550 \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv generic

# Sky130 ASIC synthesis
bash scripts/bash/synth_yosys.sh uart_16550 \
    rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv sky130

# Direct Yosys invocation
yosys -s eda/yosys/synth_sky130.ys

docs.title: 8.2.3 Reading the Statistics Output
docs.text:
After synthesis, Yosys prints a statistics summary:

=== uart_16550 ===

   Number of wires:               1234
   Number of wire bits:           5678
   Number of public wires:          45
   Number of cells:               812
     sky130_fd_sc_hd__a21oi_2      48    <- AND-OR-INVERT gate
     sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_2     216    <- D flip-flop
     sky130_fd_sc_hd__inv_2        89    <- Inverter
     sky130_fd_sc_hd__mux2_4       34    <- 2-input mux
     sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_4      78    -- and more...

   Chip area for module 'uart_16550': 47,832 um^2
   (approx. 0.048 mm^2 in Sky130A)

Interpreting the numbers:

  • The 216 DFF cells correspond to the flip-flops in the UART’s TX/RX FIFOs, state machines, and registers.

  • The 48 mm\(^2\) area is about 6.9 mm \(\times\) 6.9 mm — tiny compared to the full Caravel user project area of 2.65 mm \(\times\) 2.92 mm.

  • The cell count (812) is a measure of design complexity. A simple processor like PicoRV32 is \(\sim\)2500 cells; a CVA6 is \(\sim\)100,000 cells.

docs.title: 8.3 Vivado Synthesis (FPGA)
docs.text:
For Xilinx FPGAs, Vivado’s synthesis maps to LUTs instead of standard cells. The relevant commands are inside fpga/xilinx-artix7/build_arty_a7.tcl:

synth_design \
    -top uart_16550 \
    -part xc7a35ticsg324-1L \      # Target device
    -flatten_hierarchy rebuilt \   # Flatten for optimisation
    -fsm_extraction one_hot \      # One-hot FSM encoding
    -directive PerformanceOptimized # Prioritise speed over area

docs.title: 8.3.1 Synthesis Directives
docs.text: Table 8.1. Vivado synth_design directives Directive Effect Default Balanced speed and area PerformanceOptimized Maximum timing performance, ignores area AreaOptimized_medium Reduce LUT count at the cost of timing RuntimeOptimized Fast synthesis for quick checks (less optimal result) AlternateRoutability Change netlist to improve place-and-route

docs.title: 8.4 Understanding the Netlist
docs.text:
After synthesis, you have a gate-level netlist. Here is a tiny fragment of what the UART FSM looks like after mapping to Sky130A cells:

// Auto-generated by Yosys --- do not edit!
// This is what the synthesis tool produces from your FSM code.

// Flip-flop for state bit [0]
sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_2 \tx_state_reg[0] (
    .D  (\tx_state[0]$next ),
    .Q  (tx_state[0]),
    .CLK(clk)
);

// NAND gate for next-state logic
sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_4 \tx_nxt[0] (
    .A(tx_state[1]),
    .B(\baud_tick ),
    .Y(\tx_state[0]$next_n )
);

// Inverter
sky130_fd_sc_hd__inv_2 \tx_inv[0] (
    .A(\tx_state[0]$next_n ),
    .X(\tx_state[0]$next )
);

This is not intended to be human-readable — it is the input to the physical design tools.

docs.title: 8.5 Liberty Files — Describing Standard Cells
docs.text:
The liberty file (.lib) is the synthesis tool’s bible for a given technology. It describes every cell:

cell (sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_4) {
    area : 3.745;              /* Cell area in um^2 */
    cell_leakage_power : 0.012; /* Static power in uW */

    pin (A) { direction : input; }
    pin (B) { direction : input; }
    pin (Y) {
        direction    : output;
        function     : "!(A B)";   /* Y = NOT(A AND B) */
        timing () {
            related_pin       : "A";
            cell_rise (template_7x7) { /* Lookup table for
                values("0.0128, 0.0322, ..."); /* rise delay */
            }
            cell_fall (template_7x7) { ... }
        }
    }
}

The timing tables allow the synthesis (and later the STA) tool to calculate the exact propagation delay through any combination of cells.

docs.title: 8.6 ABC — The Logic Optimiser
docs.text:
ABC (A System for Sequential Synthesis and Verification) is the optimisation engine inside Yosys. It applies hundreds of Boolean optimisation passes to minimise the number of cells while meeting timing constraints:

# Tells ABC that the target clock period is 10 ns (100 MHz)
# so it knows which paths are critical
set_driving_cell sky130_fd_sc_hd__buf_4

# Maximum output load
set_load 0.5

# Target clock period for timing-driven optimisation
clock 10.0

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Synthesis translates RTL (SystemVerilog) into a gate netlist.

  • Yosys is the open-source synthesis tool used for Sky130/GF180 ASIC flows.

  • Vivado synthesis maps to Xilinx LUTs for FPGA targets.

  • The liberty file (.lib) describes cell timing, area, and power.

  • ABC is the core logic optimiser — it minimises cells while meeting the target clock period.

  • After synthesis you have a gate netlist — the input to physical design (Chapter 9).

docs.title: Chapter 9: Physical Design
docs.text:
Physical design turns the gate netlist produced by synthesis into an exact physical layout: where each cell sits on silicon, which metal layer connects them, and how the clock reaches every flip-flop at exactly the right moment.

Analogy: Physical Design as Urban Planning

The gate netlist is like a list of buildings and roads in a city. Physical design is the city planner’s job: decide where every building goes (placement), lay out the road network (routing), ensure power reaches every building (PDN), and synchronise all traffic lights (clock tree synthesis).

docs.title: 9.1 The Physical Design Flow
docs.text: Figure 9.1. Physical design flow — all steps run with OpenROAD

docs.title: 9.2 OpenROAD — The Open-Source Physical Design Suite
docs.text:
OpenROAD is a complete, open-source RTL-to-GDSII physical design tool maintained by UC San Diego and a community of contributors. It is the engine inside OpenLane (the automated flow from Efabless).

The complete flow script is at eda/openroad/full_flow.tcl.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Step 1: Floorplan
docs.text:
The floorplan defines the die boundary (the chip outline) and the core area (where cells can be placed), and places I/O pins around the edge.

# Option A: Fixed die size (500 um x 500 um, 10 um core margin)
initialize_floorplan \
    -die_area  {0 0 500 500} \
    -core_area {10 10 490 490} \
    -site      sky130_fd_sc_hd__unit

# Option B: Auto-size from target utilisation
initialize_floorplan \
    -utilization  0.45 \          # Fill 45
    -aspect_ratio 1.0 \           # Square chip
    -core_space   10 \            # 10 um margin to die edge
    -site         sky130_fd_sc_hd__unit

# Place I/O pins randomly (for initial testing)
place_pins -hor_layers {met2} -ver_layers {met3} -random

Choosing Target Utilisation

  • 30–45%: Easy routing, good timing. Large chip.

  • 45–60%: Balanced (recommended starting point).

  • 60–75%: Tight routing. Routing DRC violations common.

  • >75%: Typically unroutable. Reduce utilisation.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Step 2: Power Distribution Network (PDN)
docs.text:
Every cell needs a stable power supply. The PDN consists of:

  • Power rings: thick metal rings around the core boundary.

  • Power stripes: regular metal tracks crossing the core.

  • Standard cell rails: horizontal VDD/VSS rails in MET1 connecting directly to cell power pins.

# Define the power domain
set_voltage_domain -name CORE -power VDD -ground VSS

# Create the PDN grid template
define_pdn_grid -name main_grid \
    -voltage_domains CORE -starts_with POWER

# Ring around core: 3 um wide on MET4 and MET5
add_pdn_ring -grid main_grid \
    -layers {met4 met5} \
    -widths {3.0 3.0} \
    -spacings {2.0 2.0}

# Internal horizontal stripes on MET4 every 50 um
add_pdn_stripe -grid main_grid \
    -layer met4 -width 1.6 -pitch 50.0 -offset 5

# Internal vertical stripes on MET5 every 50 um
add_pdn_stripe -grid main_grid \
    -layer met5 -width 1.6 -pitch 50.0 -offset 5

# Connect MET4 stripes to MET5 stripes via VIA4
add_pdn_connect -grid main_grid -layers {met4 met5}

# Generate the PDN (creates actual geometry)
pdngen

docs.title: 9.2.3 Step 3: Placement
docs.text:
The placer assigns each cell a legal position on the placement grid. It minimises wirelength (shorter wires = less delay, less power).

# Global placement: approximate positions
global_placement \
    -density 0.55 \       # Target cell density
    -pad_left 2 \         # Padding at core boundary
    -pad_right 2

# Detailed placement: legalise all overlaps
detailed_placement
check_placement -verbose   # Report any violations

# Estimate wire parasitics (needed for timing-driven optimisation)
estimate_parasitics -placement

# Insert buffers on long nets (>500 um)
repair_design -max_wire_length 500

docs.title: 9.2.4 Step 4: Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS)
docs.text:
CTS builds a balanced clock distribution network that delivers the clock signal to every flip-flop with minimal skew (difference in arrival time).

clock_tree_synthesis \
    -root_buf   sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16 \  # Root buffer (largest)
    -buf_list   {sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4    # Branch buffers
                 sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_8
                 sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16} \
    -sink_clustering_enable \    # Group nearby sinks to share buffers
    -sink_clustering_size 20     # Max 20 sinks per cluster

# After CTS, propagate clock timing
set_propagated_clock [all_clocks]

# Fix long clock nets inserted by CTS
repair_clock_nets -max_wire_length 100

# Re-legalise placement after CTS adds buffers
detailed_placement
Figure 9.2. Clock tree: balanced binary tree of buffers minimises skew across all FFs

docs.title: 9.2.5 Step 5: Routing
docs.text:
Routing assigns actual metal wires to all the logical connections in the netlist. It works in two phases:

Global routing Plans which regions each wire passes through, layer by layer. Detailed routing Assigns exact wire paths on each metal layer, respecting minimum width and spacing design rules. 
# Global routing
global_route \
    -guide_file grt_guide.txt \
    -overflow_iterations 100

# Detailed routing
detailed_route \
    -output_drc gdsii/outputs/route_drc.rpt \
    -droute_end_iter 64

# Check for remaining design rule violations
check_antennas -report_violating_nets

# Fix antenna violations by inserting diodes
repair_antennas sky130_fd_sc_hd__diode_2
check_antennas   # Verify no remaining antenna violations

Antenna Effect Explained

During manufacturing, metal layers are deposited one at a time. A long piece of metal connected to a transistor gate, but with its other end not yet connected, can accumulate electrical charge during plasma etching. This charge can permanently damage the gate oxide. The fix is to add a diode near the gate as a charge bleeder. OpenROAD inserts these automatically with repair_antennas.

docs.title: 9.3 Parasitic Extraction and Final STA
docs.text:
After routing, the actual wire lengths and capacitances are known. The tool extracts a SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) file and runs a final timing analysis:

# Extract RC parasitics from routed layout
extract_parasitics \
    -spef_file gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.spef

# Load parasitics for accurate timing analysis
read_spef gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.spef

# Final timing report (must show no violations)
report_checks -path_delay max -group_count 20
report_check_types -max_setup -max_hold

docs.title: 9.3.1 Reading Timing Paths
docs.text:
A typical timing path report looks like this:

Startpoint: tx_state_reg[0] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Endpoint:   uart_txd_reg    (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Path Group: clk
Path Type:  max (Setup)

       Cap   Slew  Delay   Time   Description
------------------------------------------------------------------------
              0.00  0.00   0.00 ^ clock clk (rise edge)
                    0.19   0.19 ^ clock network delay (propagated)
              0.00  0.00   0.19 ^ tx_state_reg[0]/CLK (sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_2)
              0.68  0.44   0.63 ^ tx_state_reg[0]/Q (sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_2)
0.022  0.03  0.03   0.66 ^ U_nand1/Y (sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_4)
0.019  0.02  0.08   0.74 v U_inv1/Y  (sky130_fd_sc_hd__inv_2)
0.044  0.06  0.16   0.90 ^ U_mux1/X  (sky130_fd_sc_hd__mux2_4)
              0.12   1.02 ^ uart_txd_reg/D (sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_2)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
              0.28         data arrival time (1.02 ns)
10.00          10.00       clock clk (rise edge)
              0.19         clock network delay (propagated)
             -0.35         clock uncertainty
              9.84         clock arrival time
             -0.16         library setup time
              9.68         data required time
------------------------------------------------------------------------
              8.66         slack (MET)   <- Positive = PASS

The slack of 8.66 ns means there is 8.66 ns to spare in this path — the timing constraint is comfortably met.

docs.title: 9.4 GDSII — The Final Output
docs.text:
After routing and DRC, the tool writes the GDSII file — the standard format that foundries use to manufacture chips.

# Write GDSII (stream out layout)
write_gds gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.gds

# Write final gate netlist (with cell names mapped back)
write_verilog gdsii/outputs/uart_16550_final.v

# Write final SDC (timing constraints with propagated clocks)
write_sdc gdsii/outputs/uart_16550_final.sdc

klayout gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.gds \
    -l $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/klayout/sky130A.lyp

# Check GDS structure with Python
python3 gdsii/scripts/gds_check.py gdsii/outputs/uart_16550.gds

docs.title: 9.5 OpenLane — Fully Automated RTL-to-GDS
docs.text:
OpenLane 2 wraps all the OpenROAD steps into a single, automated flow driven by a JSON configuration file:

# Install
pip install openlane

# Run (reads pipeline/configs/openlane_config.json)
python3 -m openlane \
    --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
    --pdk sky130A \
    pipeline/configs/openlane_config.json

# Outputs in: runs/<timestamp>/
#   final/gds/uart_16550.gds
#   final/lef/uart_16550.lef
#   reports/signoff/timing.rpt

{
    "DESIGN_NAME": "uart_16550",
    "VERILOG_FILES": ["rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv"],
    "CLOCK_PORT": "clk",
    "CLOCK_PERIOD": 10.0,
    "PDK": "sky130A",
    "STD_CELL_LIBRARY": "sky130_fd_sc_hd",

    "FP_CORE_UTIL": 45,
    "PL_TARGET_DENSITY": 0.55,
    "ROUTING_CORES": 8
}

docs.title: 9.6 Summary
docs.text:
• Physical design turns a gate netlist into exact silicon geometry.

  • Floorplan: define die size, core area, I/O positions.

  • PDN: lay power rings and stripes to deliver VDD/VSS.

  • Placement: position each cell; target 45–60% utilisation.

  • CTS: build a balanced clock tree (skew \(<\) 100 ps).

  • Routing: assign metal wires; fix antenna violations.

  • SPEF + STA: extract parasitics, verify timing (WNS \(\geq\) 0).

  • GDSII: the final layout file sent to the foundry.

  • OpenLane 2 automates all steps from a single config file.

docs.title: Chapter 10: PDKs and Fabrication
docs.text:
Every time a chip designer runs synthesis or place-and-route, the tools need detailed information about the manufacturing process: How thick are the metal layers? How fast is a NAND gate? How much leakage current does a flip-flop have? This information is packaged into a Process Design Kit (PDK).

Analogy: PDK as a Builder’s Catalogue

When an architect designs a building, they choose materials from a supplier’s catalogue: “Steel beam grade A36, yield strength 250 MPa, cost $X per tonne.” A PDK is exactly that catalogue for transistors and metal wires. It tells the design tools exactly what the foundry can make, how fast each cell switches, how much power it draws, and what design rules must not be violated.

docs.title: 10.1 The Three PDKs Used in This Project
docs.text:
Table 10.1. PDKs supported by this project PDK Foundry Node Cost Min gate (nm) sky130A SkyWater / Google 130nm Free (MPW shuttle) 150 gf180mcuD GlobalFoundries 180nm Free (MPW shuttle) 180 asap7 Academic (ASU) 7nm Free (simulation only) 7

Sky130A is the recommended PDK for beginners. It is fully open source, well documented, and backed by a free tapeout programme (see Section 10.7).

docs.title: 10.2 What Is Inside a PDK?
docs.text: A PDK contains several categories of files:

docs.title: 10.2.1 Standard Cell Library
docs.text:
The standard cell library is the collection of basic logic gates and flip-flops that the synthesis tool uses. For Sky130A, the library is called sky130_fd_sc_hd (High Density).

Table 10.2. Files in a standard cell library File type Extension Used for Liberty timing file .lib / .db Synthesis timing constraints, STA LEF abstract view .lef Cell bounding box and pin locations GDS layout view .gds Final physical shape for each cell Verilog model .v Functional simulation after synthesis SPICE netlist .sp Transistor-level simulation

A Liberty file entry for a 2-input NAND gate looks like:

cell (sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1) {
    area : 3.75;              /* area in um^2 */
    cell_leakage_power : 0.0031;
    pin(A) { direction : input; }
    pin(B) { direction : input; }
    pin(Y) {
        direction : output;
        function : "!(A&B)";
        timing() {
            related_pin : "A";
            cell_rise(delay_template_7x7) {
                /* 7x7 table: input slew vs. output load */
                values ("0.028, 0.053, ...", ...);
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 10.2.2 Design Rule Check (DRC) Rules
docs.text:
DRC rules define the geometric constraints that the foundry’s photolithography process imposes. Violating them means the chip cannot be manufactured correctly.

Table 10.3. Common DRC rule categories Rule type What it checks Minimum width Metal/poly wires must be at least \(N\) nm wide Minimum spacing Adjacent wires must have at least \(N\) nm gap Minimum enclosure Via must be enclosed by at least \(N\) nm of metal Minimum area Metal regions below a minimum area must not exist Density Metal fill must cover between X% and Y% of each tile

For Sky130A, the DRC rules are checked with Magic VLSI or KLayout:

# Using Magic VLSI
magic -rcfile $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/magic/sky130A.magicrc \
      -noconsole -dnull << 'EOF'
gds read /path/to/design.gds
load design
drc check
drc catchup
quit
EOF

# Using KLayout (faster for large designs)
klayout -b -r $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/klayout/drc/sky130A.lydrc \
        -rd input=/path/to/design.gds \
        -rd report=/path/to/drc_report.xml

docs.title: 10.2.3 Layout vs. Schematic (LVS)
docs.text:
LVS compares the physical layout (extracted from GDS) against the logical netlist to make sure they describe the same circuit. This catches situations where a wire was accidentally deleted or a via was missing.

# Extract SPICE netlist from layout
magic -rcfile $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/magic/sky130A.magicrc \
      -noconsole -dnull << 'EOF'
gds read /path/to/design.gds
load design
extract all
ext2spice lvs
ext2spice
quit
EOF

# Compare extracted netlist to schematic netlist with Netgen
netgen -batch lvs \
    "/path/to/design.ext.spice design" \
    "/path/to/synthesis.spice design" \
    $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/netgen/sky130A_setup.tcl \
    /path/to/lvs_report.txt

Passing DRC + LVS is the minimum requirement before any chip is submitted for fabrication. They are collectively called signoff checks.

docs.title: 10.3 Sky130A — The Free 130nm PDK
docs.text: Sky130A was released as open source in 2020 through a partnership between SkyWater Technology (a US foundry) and Google. It is the first commercial PDK released without an NDA.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Layer Stack
docs.text:
Sky130A uses 5 metal layers plus local interconnect:

Table 10.4. Sky130A metal layer stack Layer Name in PDK Purpose Min width (nm) Local Interconnect li1 Cell-level wiring 170 Metal 1 met1 Primary signal routing 140 Metal 2 met2 Secondary signal routing 140 Metal 3 met3 Regional routing 300 Metal 4 met4 Long horizontal wires 300 Metal 5 met5 Power rails 1600

docs.title: 10.3.2 Setting Up the PDK
docs.text:
# Install volare (PDK version manager)
pip install volare

# Fetch the Sky130A PDK
export PDK_ROOT=$HOME/pdks
volare enable --pdk sky130 \
    --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
    bdc9412b3e468c102d01b7cf6337be06ec6e9c9a

# Verify installation
ls $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.ref/sky130_fd_sc_hd/
# Should show: lib/  lef/  gds/  verilog/  spice/

docs.title: 10.4 GF180MCU — GlobalFoundries 180nm
docs.text:
The GF180MCU PDK supports GlobalFoundries’ 180nm CMOS process, which is optimised for microcontroller and mixed-signal designs. It provides:

  • 5V and 3.3V I/O cells

  • Precision resistors and MIM capacitors

  • EEPROM-compatible process options

  • Four standard-cell libraries (HD, HS, HV, LV)

export PDK_ROOT=$HOME/pdks
volare enable --pdk gf180mcu \
    --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
    e0f692f46654d6c7c99fc70a0c94a080dab53571

docs.title: 10.5 ASAP7 — Academic 7nm PDK
docs.text:
ASAP7 is an academic PDK developed by Arizona State University (ASU) and ARM Research. It models a realistic 7nm FinFET process but is intended for research and education only — not for actual fabrication. It is useful for studying how area, power, and timing scale from 130nm to 7nm.

Table 10.5. 130nm vs 7nm key metrics (same NAND2 gate) Metric Sky130A (130nm) ASAP7 (7nm) NAND2 cell area 3.75 m\(^2\) 0.038 m\(^2\) NAND2 cell delay \(\sim\)100 ps \(\sim\)5 ps VDD 1.8 V 0.7 V Max frequency \(\sim\)250 MHz \(\sim\)3 GHz 
# OpenROAD config for ASAP7 (from pdk/asap7/asap7_openroad_config.mk)
export PDK=asap7
export PLATFORM=asap7
export TECH_LEF=$PDK_ROOT/asap7/tech/asap7_tech_1x_201209.lef
export SC_LEF=$PDK_ROOT/asap7/lib/asap7sc7p5t_28_R_1x_220121a.lef
export LIB_FILES=$PDK_ROOT/asap7/lib/asap7sc7p5t_SEQ_RVT_TT_nldm_220123.lib

docs.title: 10.6 The Tapeout Process
docs.text: A tapeout is the point at which a design is submitted to the foundry for manufacturing. The term dates from the era when chip data was literally written onto magnetic tape for delivery to the fab.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Steps to Tapeout
docs.text:
1. Design Freeze: All features locked, no more RTL changes.

  2. Full LVS + DRC Clean: Zero violations on the complete chip.

  3. Antenna Check Clean: All antenna violations resolved.

  4. Density Fill: Metal fill added to reach required density.

  5. Final STA: Setup and hold checks pass at all corners.

  6. GDS Merge: All IP blocks merged into single top-level GDS.

  7. Final DRC on Merged GDS: Full-chip DRC one last time.

  8. Submit: GDS + LEF + Netlist sent to foundry.

Tapeout Is Irreversible — Check Everything Twice

Once a chip is submitted, it takes 8–16 weeks to come back from the foundry. Any bug in the design is “baked in” permanently. There is no patch, no firmware update. This is why verification (Chapter 7) and signoff checks are taken so seriously. Professional teams run DRC/LVS dozens of times before tapeout.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Corner Analysis
docs.text:
Chips must work across a range of process, voltage, and temperature variations. This is called PVT corner analysis.

Table 10.6. Standard PVT corners for 1.8V Sky130A designs Corner Process Voltage Temperature TT (Typical-Typical) Nominal Nominal \(25^{\circ}\)C FF (Fast-Fast) Fastest 1.98V \(-40^{\circ}\)C SS (Slow-Slow) Slowest 1.62V \(125^{\circ}\)C FS (Fast-Slow) Fast-N / Slow-P Nominal \(25^{\circ}\)C SF (Slow-Fast) Slow-N / Fast-P Nominal \(25^{\circ}\)C

The SS corner at \(125^{\circ}\)C is used for setup time checks (slowest logic). The FF corner at \(-40^{\circ}\)C is used for hold time checks (fastest logic, clock arrives early, data may overtake it).

docs.title: 10.7 Efabless and the MPW Shuttle
docs.text: Efabless runs a programme called the Multi-Project Wafer (MPW) shuttle that allows individual designers to tapeout a chip for free (or at very low cost). Multiple designers share a single wafer run.

docs.title: 10.7.1 The Caravel Harness
docs.text:
Every design submitted to the Efabless MPW must be wrapped inside a standard template called the Caravel harness. Caravel provides:

  • A RISC-V (PicoRV32) management core for chip configuration.

  • 38 general-purpose I/O (GPIO) pins with configurable direction.

  • A 2.4 mm \(\times\) 2.4 mm user project area for your design.

  • A Wishbone bus and Logic Analyser (LA) connection to the management core.

Figure 10.1. Efabless Caravel harness structure

docs.title: 10.7.2 Submitting to MPW
docs.text:
# 1. Clone the Caravel user project template
git clone https://github.com/efabless/caravel_user_project

# 2. Copy your design into user_project_wrapper
#    (your GDS must fit inside the 2.4mm x 2.4mm area)
cp my_design.gds caravel_user_project/gds/

# 3. Run the full OpenLane hardening flow
cd caravel_user_project
make user_project_wrapper

# 4. Run the Efabless pre-check (mandatory before submission)
make precheck

# 5. If precheck passes, submit via the Efabless platform
# (web dashboard at efabless.com)

docs.title: 10.8 Reading a GDSII File
docs.text:
GDSII (Graphic Design System II) is the standard file format for chip layouts. It contains polygons, paths, and cell instances organised into a hierarchical structure.

# Open GDS in KLayout GUI
klayout /path/to/design.gds

# In KLayout: Layer panel shows all layers (met1, met2, poly, ndiff...)
# Use Ctrl+F to search for cell names
# Ruler tool (R) to measure distances

# Extract area statistics from command line
klayout -b -r - << 'EOF'
layout = RBA::Layout.new
layout.read("/path/to/design.gds")
layout.each_cell { |cell|
  puts "#{cell.name}: #{cell.bbox}"
}
EOF

# Merge multiple GDS files (from gdsii/scripts/gds_merge.py)
python gdsii/scripts/gds_merge.py \
    --top  top_level.gds \
    --subs my_design.gds \
    --out  merged.gds

docs.title: 10.9 Metal Fill and Density Rules
docs.text:
Most foundries require the metal density in every 100m \(\times\) 100m tile to fall between a minimum (typically 20%) and maximum (typically 80%). If your design is sparse, the tools insert floating metal fill — small, electrically isolated metal squares — to meet the density requirement.

# Run density fill for all metal layers
detailed_placement
check_placement -verbose
density_fill \
    -rules $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/openlane/rules.fill.tcl
write_def design_with_fill.def

Fill Affects Capacitance

Metal fill is electrically floating but adds parasitic capacitance to nearby signal wires. For high-speed designs, extract parasitics after fill insertion and re-run STA to verify timing is not degraded.

docs.title: 10.10 The Signoff Checklist
docs.text:
The file gdsii/drc-lvs/drc_checklist.md in this project contains the full tapeout checklist. The key items are:

  1. DRC: Zero errors in Magic and KLayout.

  2. LVS: Netlist matches layout, zero mismatches.

  3. Antenna: Zero antenna violations (or approved waives).

  4. ERC: No floating gates, no latch-up paths.

  5. STA — Setup: WNS \(\geq 0\) at SS/\(125^{\circ}\)C corner.

  6. STA — Hold: WNS \(\geq 0\) at FF/\(-40^{\circ}\)C corner.

  7. Density: All tile densities between 20% and 80%.

  8. IR Drop: Maximum rail drop \(< 5\%\) VDD.

  9. GDS: File opens cleanly in KLayout, all layers present.

  10. Functional: Simulation passes on extracted (post-layout) netlist.

docs.title: 10.11 Summary
docs.text:
• A PDK packages everything the tools need to know about a manufacturing process: timing, area, rules, layer stacks.

  • Sky130A is free and open-source — the recommended starting point for anyone new to ASIC design.

  • DRC and LVS checks are mandatory before tapeout; failing either means the chip cannot be manufactured.

  • PVT corner analysis ensures the design works in the worst-case combination of process variation, voltage, and temperature.

  • The Efabless MPW shuttle lets individuals tapeout real chips at no cost using the Caravel harness wrapper.

  • GDSII is the final output format; tools like KLayout and Magic are used to view and verify it.

The next and final chapter covers how all these steps are automated together into a single, reproducible pipeline.

docs.title: Chapter 11: The Automation Pipeline
docs.text:
By now you have seen every stage of the FPGA/ASIC design flow: from writing RTL in SystemVerilog, through simulation and synthesis, to place-and-route and tapeout signoff. In practice, running these stages manually — typing commands one by one — is impractical for real projects. A single design change might require re-running synthesis, re-running PnR, re-running STA, and re-running DRC/LVS.

This chapter shows how the project automates the entire flow with Python scripts, Makefiles, and a master orchestration engine.

Analogy: The Automation Pipeline as a Factory Assembly Line

Imagine a car factory. Each workstation performs one operation: weld the frame, install the engine, paint the body. The conveyor belt connects them all, moving each car automatically from one station to the next without human intervention. The automation pipeline in this project is that conveyor belt — a shell command triggers the whole flow, and the output is a GDS or bitstream with no manual steps in between.

docs.title: 11.1 The Big Picture
docs.text: Figure 11.1. Master automation pipeline — one command, full flow

docs.title: 11.2 The Makefile Entry Point
docs.text:
The file scripts/makefile/Makefile is the user-facing entry point. It exposes simple commands that chain together the Python scripts and shell scripts beneath.

# Prototype an IP block on FPGA (Arty A7)
make ip IP=uart_16550 TARGET=fpga BOARD=arty_a7_35t

# Run full ASIC flow to GDSII (Sky130A)
make ip IP=uart_16550 TARGET=asic PDK=sky130

# Run simulation only
make sim IP=uart_16550

# Run linting only
make lint IP=uart_16550

# Run formal verification
make formal IP=uart_16550

# Clean all build artefacts
make clean IP=uart_16550

# Generate a new IP stub from a YAML specification
make gen SPEC=pipeline/templates/ip_spec_template.yaml

# Default PDK and board
PDK   ?= sky130
BOARD ?= arty_a7_35t

ip: lint sim
ifeq ($(TARGET), fpga)
    bash scripts/bash/fpga_build.sh $(IP) $(BOARD)
else ifeq ($(TARGET), asic)
    python pipeline/automation/ip_pipeline.py \
        --ip $(IP) --pdk $(PDK) --target asic
endif

lint:
    bash scripts/bash/lint_check.sh rtl-templates/

sim:
    bash scripts/bash/sim_run.sh \
        rtl-templates/peripherals/$(IP).sv \
        verification/tb-templates/$(IP)_tb.sv tb

gen:
    python scripts/python/ip_generator.py --spec $(SPEC)

.PHONY: ip lint sim gen formal clean

docs.title: 11.3 The Python Orchestrator
docs.text: The file pipeline/automation/ip_pipeline.py is the master orchestration script. It reads a YAML specification for an IP block and drives the entire flow programmatically.

docs.title: 11.3.1 How the Orchestrator Works
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
ip_pipeline.py --- Master RTL-to-GDSII / RTL-to-Bitstream orchestrator.
Usage: python ip_pipeline.py --ip uart_16550 --pdk sky130 --target asic
"""
import subprocess, sys, pathlib, yaml, argparse, logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

STAGES_ASIC = ["lint", "sim", "synth_yosys", "floorplan",
               "placement", "cts", "routing", "sta", "drc_lvs"]
STAGES_FPGA = ["lint", "sim", "vivado_synth", "vivado_impl",
               "vivado_bitstream"]

def run(cmd: list, cwd=None) -> int:
    """Run a shell command; return exit code."""
    log.info("Running:
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=cwd)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        log.error("FAILED at stage:
        sys.exit(result.returncode)
    return 0

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--ip",     required=True, help="IP block name")
    parser.add_argument("--pdk",    default="sky130")
    parser.add_argument("--target", choices=["asic", "fpga"], default="asic")
    parser.add_argument("--board",  default="arty_a7_35t")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    stages = STAGES_ASIC if args.target == "asic" else STAGES_FPGA
    log.info("Starting pipeline: ip=
             args.ip, args.pdk, args.target)

    for stage in stages:
        if   stage == "lint":
            run(["bash", "scripts/bash/lint_check.sh",
                 f"rtl-templates/peripherals/{args.ip}.sv"])
        elif stage == "sim":
            run(["bash", "scripts/bash/sim_run.sh",
                 f"rtl-templates/peripherals/{args.ip}.sv",
                 f"verification/tb-templates/{args.ip}_tb.sv", "tb"])
        elif stage == "synth_yosys":
            run(["bash", "scripts/bash/synth_yosys.sh",
                 args.ip,
                 f"rtl-templates/peripherals/{args.ip}.sv",
                 args.pdk])
        elif stage == "floorplan":
            run(["openroad", "-exit",
                 f"eda/openroad/{args.ip}/floorplan.tcl"])
        # ... (remaining stages follow the same pattern)

    log.info("Pipeline complete --- all stages passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                        format="
    main()

docs.title: 11.4 IP Generation from YAML Specification
docs.text: The file scripts/python/ip_generator.py generates SystemVerilog RTL stubs, register maps, and testbench skeletons from a compact YAML specification. This saves hours of boilerplate typing.

docs.title: 11.4.1 The IP Specification Format
docs.text:
# IP block specification --- edit and run `make gen SPEC=this_file.yaml`
name:         my_counter
description:  "32-bit AXI4-Lite addressable counter"
version:      "1.0"
author:       "your_name"

interface: axi4_lite          # axi4_lite | wishbone | apb | native
data_width: 32
addr_width: 5
clock:  clk
reset:  rst_n
reset_polarity: active_low

registers:
  - name:   COUNT
    offset: 0x00
    access: RO                # RO | RW | WO | W1C
    reset:  0x00000000
    fields:
      - name: value
        bits: "31:0"
        description: "Current counter value"

  - name:   CTRL
    offset: 0x04
    access: RW
    reset:  0x00000000
    fields:
      - name: enable
        bits: "0"
        description: "Set 1 to enable counting"
      - name: clear
        bits: "1"
        description: "Write 1 to reset counter to 0"

parameters:
  - name:  COUNT_WIDTH
    value: 32
    description: "Bit width of counter"

docs.title: 11.4.2 What the Generator Produces
docs.text:
Running make gen SPEC=my_spec.yaml creates:

  1. rtl-templates/peripherals/my_counter.sv — AXI4-Lite slave with all registers pre-wired.

  2. verification/tb-templates/my_counter_tb.sv — Testbench skeleton with AXI4-Lite write/read tasks.

  3. docs/my_counter_regmap.md — Human-readable register map.

  4. ip-library/my_counter/my_counter.core — FuseSoC descriptor.

def generate_sv(spec: dict, out_path: pathlib.Path):
    """Generate SystemVerilog AXI4-Lite slave from YAML spec."""
    regs = spec["registers"]
    n_regs = len(regs)
    dw = spec.get("data_width", 32)
    aw = spec.get("addr_width", 5)
    name = spec["name"]

    lines = []
    lines.append(f"// Auto-generated by ip_generator.py --- DO NOT EDIT")
    lines.append(f"module {name} #(")
    for p in spec.get("parameters", []):
        lines.append(f"    parameter int {p['name']} = {p['value']},")
    lines.append(f") (")
    lines.append(f"    input  logic                clk,")
    lines.append(f"    input  logic                rst_n,")
    lines.append(f"    // AXI4-Lite slave ports")
    lines.append(f"    input  logic [{aw}-1:0]      s_axi_awaddr,")
    # ... (remaining ports follow)
    lines.append(f");")
    lines.append(f"")
    lines.append(f"    // Register array")
    lines.append(f"    logic [{dw}-1:0] regs [0:{n_regs-1}];")
    # ... (write/read logic follows)
    lines.append(f"endmodule")
    out_path.write_text("\n".join(lines))

docs.title: 11.5 Register Map Generator
docs.text:
The file scripts/python/regmap_gen.py takes the same YAML specification and generates documentation in Markdown, HTML, or C header format — making it easy to share the register map with software engineers writing firmware.

# Markdown (for documentation)
python scripts/python/regmap_gen.py \
    --spec pipeline/templates/ip_spec_template.yaml \
    --format markdown \
    --out docs/my_counter_regmap.md

# C header (for firmware drivers)
python scripts/python/regmap_gen.py \
    --spec pipeline/templates/ip_spec_template.yaml \
    --format c_header \
    --out firmware/include/my_counter_regs.h

# HTML (for web documentation)
python scripts/python/regmap_gen.py \
    --spec pipeline/templates/ip_spec_template.yaml \
    --format html \
    --out docs/my_counter_regmap.html

The generated C header looks like:

/* my_counter_regs.h --- Auto-generated by regmap_gen.py */
#ifndef MY_COUNTER_REGS_H
#define MY_COUNTER_REGS_H

#define MY_COUNTER_BASE    0x30000000UL

/* COUNT --- Current counter value (RO) */
#define MY_COUNTER_COUNT_OFFSET    0x00
#define MY_COUNTER_COUNT_ADDR      (MY_COUNTER_BASE + 0x00)

/* CTRL --- Control register (RW) */
#define MY_COUNTER_CTRL_OFFSET     0x04
#define MY_COUNTER_CTRL_ADDR       (MY_COUNTER_BASE + 0x04)
#define MY_COUNTER_CTRL_ENABLE_BIT 0
#define MY_COUNTER_CTRL_CLEAR_BIT  1

#endif /* MY_COUNTER_REGS_H */

docs.title: 11.6 FuseSoC — IP Package Manager
docs.text:
FuseSoC is the package manager for hardware IP. It reads .core descriptor files and manages dependencies between IP blocks, just as pip does for Python packages.

# Add the local IP library as a FuseSoC library
fusesoc library add fpga-asic-pipeline .

# List all available cores
fusesoc list-cores

# Run simulation of a specific core
fusesoc run --target sim myorg:uart_16550:1.0

# Synthesise for a specific FPGA target
fusesoc run --target arty_a7_35t myorg:uart_16550:1.0

A .core file for the UART looks like:

CAPI=2:
name: myorg:uart_16550:1.0
description: UART 16550-compatible with AXI4-Lite interface

filesets:
  rtl:
    files:
      - ../../rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv
    file_type: systemVerilogSource

  tb:
    files:
      - ../../verification/tb-templates/uart_16550_tb.sv
    file_type: systemVerilogSource
    depend:
      - myorg:axi4_lite_slave:1.0

targets:
  default:
    filesets: [rtl]

  sim:
    filesets: [rtl, tb]
    default_tool: icarus
    tools:
      icarus:
        iverilog_options: [-g2012]

docs.title: 11.7 The Complete CI Flow
docs.text:
In a professional environment, the entire pipeline runs automatically on every Git commit using Continuous Integration (CI). The project includes a GitHub Actions workflow template.

name: FPGA/ASIC CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  lint-and-sim:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Install tools
        run: |
          sudo apt-get install -y iverilog verilator
          pip install cocotb yowasp-yosys

      - name: Lint all RTL
        run: bash scripts/bash/lint_check.sh rtl-templates/

      - name: Run simulations
        run: |
          for tb in verification/tb-templates/*_tb.sv; do
            ip=$(basename $tb _tb.sv)
            bash scripts/bash/sim_run.sh \
                rtl-templates/peripherals/${ip}.sv $tb tb
          done

  synthesis-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: lint-and-sim
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Synthesise UART (generic target)
        run: |
          pip install yowasp-yosys
          bash scripts/bash/synth_yosys.sh uart_16550 \
              rtl-templates/peripherals/uart_16550.sv generic

docs.title: 11.8 Adding a New IP Block — End-to-End Walkthrough
docs.text:
Here is a complete walkthrough of adding a new SPI master peripheral to the project from scratch:

  1. Write the specification:

    cp pipeline/templates/ip_spec_template.yaml \
   pipeline/templates/spi_master_spec.yaml
# Edit spi_master_spec.yaml: add registers, parameters

  2. Generate the RTL stub:

    make gen SPEC=pipeline/templates/spi_master_spec.yaml
# Creates: rtl-templates/peripherals/spi_master.sv
#          verification/tb-templates/spi_master_tb.sv

  3. Implement the logic — fill in the RTL stub with the actual SPI FSM (CPOL/CPHA modes, shift register, chip-select logic).

  4. Lint and simulate:

    make lint IP=spi_master
make sim  IP=spi_master

  5. Add cocotb tests:

    # Create verification/cocotb/test_spi_master.py
# Test all SPI modes, test clock polarity, test byte transfer

  6. FPGA prototype:

    make ip IP=spi_master TARGET=fpga BOARD=arty_a7_35t
# Flash bitstream, test on hardware with a logic analyser

  7. ASIC flow:

    make ip IP=spi_master TARGET=asic PDK=sky130
# Full RTL -> GDSII flow; inspect results in KLayout

  8. Add to IP library:

    cp ip-library/communication/uart_16550.core \
   ip-library/communication/spi_master.core
# Edit spi_master.core: update name and file references
fusesoc list-cores  # verify it appears

docs.title: 11.10 The Agent System
docs.text:
In addition to the scripted automation, this project includes a set of AI agents — specialised AI assistants, each with deep knowledge of one stage of the design flow:

Table 11.1. AI agents in the pipeline Agent Responsibilities core-selector Recommend the right processor core given requirements rtl-design Write and review SystemVerilog RTL verification Create testbenches, cocotb tests, SVA properties fpga-proto Configure Vivado/Quartus, generate XDC/SDC constraints synthesis Run Yosys/Vivado synthesis, interpret area reports physical-design Drive OpenROAD floorplan through routing signoff Run DRC/LVS/STA, interpret violations fabrication Prepare tapeout package, Efabless submission ip-generation Generate full IP blocks from YAML specification

Each agent is invoked with a skill — a markdown file containing the agent’s prompt and tool invocations. Skills are listed in SKILLS.md and invoked with /skill-name.

docs.title: 11.11 Summary
docs.text:
• A make command triggers the entire design flow from RTL to GDSII or bitstream without any manual steps.

  • ip_pipeline.py orchestrates all stages: lint, sim, synth, PnR, STA, DRC/LVS.

  • ip_generator.py generates RTL, testbench, register map, and FuseSoC descriptor from a compact YAML specification.

  • regmap_gen.py produces C headers, Markdown docs, and HTML register maps for firmware developers.

  • FuseSoC manages IP dependencies; GitHub Actions runs the full pipeline on every commit.

  • Nine specialised AI agents cover every stage of the flow, invoked via skill files.

Congratulations — You Have Completed the Full Pipeline!

You now understand the complete journey from a hardware idea to a tapeout-ready GDSII file:

  1. Write RTL in SystemVerilog

  2. Simulate with cocotb and Verilator

  3. Lint with Verilator --lint-only

  4. Synthesise with Yosys to a gate netlist

  5. Floorplan, place, route with OpenROAD

  6. Verify timing with OpenSTA

  7. Check DRC/LVS with Magic + Netgen

  8. Package as GDSII and submit to Efabless MPW

The entire flow runs with a single make ip IP=myip TARGET=asic PDK=sky130.
